entries.meaning: Having a young-looking, round face like a child's. ---

He looks baby-faced, but he's the oldest guy on the team.
A baby-faced actor played the young president.

entries.meaning: From or relating to ancient Babylon. ---

Babylonian astronomers tracked the movements of the planets.
Experts believe the clay tablet is Babylonian.

entries.meaning: Back has 3 distinct senses.

The kids sat in the back seat.
We had coffee on the back porch.
He owes three years of back taxes.
The library keeps back issues of the magazine.
We took the back roads to avoid traffic.
They live on a quiet back street.

senses.head: At or near the rear of something
examples: Let's use the back door.
The kids sat in the back seat.
We had coffee on the back porch.

senses.head: From an earlier time; owed or published before now
examples: He owes three years of back taxes.
The library keeps back issues of the magazine.

senses.head: Away from main roads and busy places
examples: We took the back roads to avoid traffic.
They live on a quiet back street.

entries.position: attributive only — the back door; after a verb use at the back or in the back
entries.contrast: The adjective only goes before a noun: ✗ The door is back → The door is in the back. Back is much more often an adverb (come back), a noun (my back hurts) or a verb (back up).

entries.meaning: Secret and unofficial, outside the normal channels. ---
examples: The two governments held back-channel talks for months.
She used her back-channel contacts to get the information.
The deal came out of back-channel negotiations.

entries.meaning: Happening one right after the other. ---
examples: The Warriors won back-to-back championships.
I have back-to-back meetings all afternoon.
We had back-to-back snowstorms last week.
entries.contrast: As an adverb, written without hyphens, it means with backs touching (stand back to back) or one after another (two games back to back).

entries.meaning: Very hard and physically tiring. ---
examples: Picking cotton was backbreaking work.
The job was more backbreaking than I expected.
They spent a backbreaking summer building the barn.

entries.meaning: Backhanded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: 'You look great for your age' is a backhanded compliment.
She's an expert at backhanded praise.
He hit a backhanded shot down the line.
She gave him a backhanded slap.

senses.head: Seeming to praise but actually criticizing
examples: 'You look great for your age' is a backhanded compliment.
She's an expert at backhanded praise.

senses.head: Done with the back of the hand facing forward
examples: He hit a backhanded shot down the line.
She gave him a backhanded slap.

entries.meaning: Behind the stage, or private and out of public view. ---
examples: I got a backstage pass for the concert.
The documentary shows the backstage drama of a Broadway show.
There was a lot of backstage arguing before the deal was signed.
entries.contrast: More common as an adverb, stressed on the second syllable: We went backstage after the show.

entries.meaning: Backward has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She took a backward step.
He left without a backward glance.
The region was once one of the most backward in the state.
Some people still hold backward ideas about women.

senses.head: Directed toward the back or the starting point
examples: She took a backward step.
He left without a backward glance.

senses.head: Less developed or modern than others
examples: The region was once one of the most backward in the state.
Some people still hold backward ideas about women.

entries.contrast: In American English the adjective is backward; backwards is only an adverb (walk backwards), and backward can be the adverb too. Calling people or places backward sounds insulting.

entries.meaning: Caused by or relating to bacteria. ---
examples: Antibiotics only work on bacterial infections.
Strep throat is bacterial, not viral.
The lab tests water for bacterial growth.

entries.meaning: Behaving rudely; not polite. ---

It's bad-mannered to check your phone at dinner.
He was the most bad-mannered kid in the class.

entries.meaning: Easily annoyed or angry. ---
examples: Our neighbor is a bad-tempered old man.
She gets bad-tempered when she's hungry.
The meeting got more bad-tempered as it went on.

entries.meaning: Completely unable to understand something. ---
examples: Doctors were baffled by her symptoms.
He gave me a baffled look.
I'm even more baffled now than before.
entries.contrast: baffled is the person who does not understand; baffling is the thing that causes it: I was baffled by the baffling instructions.

entries.meaning: Impossible to understand or explain. ---
examples: The instructions were completely baffling.
Police called it a baffling case.
The most baffling part is that nobody saw anything.
entries.contrast: baffling is the thing; baffled is the person who does not understand it.

entries.meaning: Hanging loosely, because it is too big. ---
examples: He wore baggy jeans and a hoodie.
My pants got baggier after I lost weight.
The sweater was a little baggy on him.

entries.meaning: From or relating to the Bahamas. ---
examples: We tried Bahamian conch fritters.
The Bahamian dollar is worth the same as the US dollar.
Her mother is Bahamian.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Bahrain. ---
examples: The Bahraini government announced new visa rules.
He's Bahraini but lives in Houston.
Bahraini pearls were famous for centuries.

entries.meaning: Cooked in an oven with dry heat. ---
examples: I'll have a baked potato with sour cream.
Is the chicken fried or baked?
The church sells baked goods every Sunday.

entries.meaning: Extremely hot. ---
examples: It was baking hot inside the car.
We spent a baking hot afternoon at the ballpark.
Don't leave the dog outside; it's baking hot.
entries.contrast: An extreme adjective, so not very baking hot. Americans also just say baking: It's baking out there!

entries.meaning: Balanced has 3 distinct senses.

Viewers want balanced news coverage.

He seems well-balanced despite everything he's been through.

senses.head: Having the right amounts of different things
examples: Try to eat a balanced diet.
The team has a more balanced offense this year.

senses.head: Fair, giving all sides equal attention
examples: The article gives a balanced view of the issue.
Viewers want balanced news coverage.

senses.head: Calm and sensible
examples: She's a very balanced person.
He seems well-balanced despite everything he's been through.

entries.meaning: Bald has 3 distinct senses.

He's balder than his older brother.
A bald man in a suit opened the door.
You need new tires; these are bald.
The lawn has bald spots after the drought.
The report was a bald statement of the facts.
That's a bald lie.

senses.head: Having little or no hair on the head
examples: My dad started going bald in his thirties.
He's balder than his older brother.
A bald man in a suit opened the door.

senses.head: Worn smooth or without the usual covering
examples: You need new tires; these are bald.
The lawn has bald spots after the drought.

senses.head: Plain and direct, with nothing added to soften it
examples: The report was a bald statement of the facts.
That's a bald lie.

entries.meaning: Open and shameless, with no attempt to hide it. ---
examples: That's a bald-faced lie.
It was a bald-faced attempt to buy votes.
He told a bald-faced lie to the judge.
entries.contrast: Almost always a bald-faced lie. Barefaced means the same.

entries.meaning: Starting to lose the hair on the head. ---
examples: A balding man in his fifties sat next to me.
He's balding and a little overweight.
My uncle was already balding at twenty-five.

entries.meaning: Ballistic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The country tested a ballistic missile.
Police sent the bullets for ballistic testing.

The coach went ballistic at the referee.

senses.head: Relating to missiles or bullets and how they fly
examples: The country tested a ballistic missile.
Police sent the bullets for ballistic testing.

senses.head: Extremely angry, in go ballistic (informal)
examples: My mom went ballistic when she saw the phone bill.
The coach went ballistic at the referee.

entries.position: both — before a noun in the missile sense; after go in the angry sense

entries.meaning: Pleasantly warm, of weather or air. ---
examples: It was a balmy evening in Miami.
The weather gets balmier as you drive south.
We had the balmiest February on record.
entries.contrast: The l is silent: BAH-mee.

entries.meaning: Made with dark, sweet Italian vinegar. ---
examples: Drizzle the salad with balsamic vinegar.
The tomatoes come with a balsamic glaze.
She served the chicken with a balsamic reduction.

entries.meaning: Relating to the Baltic Sea or the countries around it. ---
examples: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are the Baltic states.

We took a cruise along the Baltic coast.

entries.meaning: Boring and ordinary, with nothing new. ---
examples: The lyrics are pretty banal.

His second book was even more banal than the first.

entries.meaning: Wrapped in a bandage. ---
examples: He came home with a bandaged hand.
Her knee was still bandaged a week after the fall.
A nurse checked the bandaged wound.

entries.meaning: Excellent (informal). ---
examples: You did a bang-up job on the kitchen.
The team had a bang-up season.
They threw a bang-up party for his retirement.
entries.position: attributive only — usually a bang-up job
entries.contrast: American informal. Not the same as banged-up, which means damaged or bruised.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Bangladesh. ---
examples: The Bangladeshi restaurants in Queens serve great curry.
He grew up in a Bangladeshi family in New York.
My coworker is Bangladeshi.

entries.meaning: Sure to make money. ---
examples: She's one of the most bankable stars in Hollywood.
Superhero movies are still bankable.
The investors didn't think the idea was bankable.

entries.meaning: Bankrupt has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The company went bankrupt in 2009.
A bankrupt airline left thousands of passengers stuck.
Critics called the government morally bankrupt.
The campaign is bankrupt of new ideas.

senses.head: Officially unable to pay one's debts
examples: The company went bankrupt in 2009.
A bankrupt airline left thousands of passengers stuck.

senses.head: Completely without a good quality
examples: Critics called the government morally bankrupt.
The campaign is bankrupt of new ideas.

entries.takes: of + noun, in the sense 'completely lacking'
entries.contrast: Say go bankrupt. Bankrupt is also a verb (The lawsuit bankrupted them) and a noun (a bankrupt).

entries.meaning: Officially not allowed. ---
examples: The athlete tested positive for a banned substance.
Fireworks are banned in this county.
He's banned from the gym for a month.

entries.meaning: Unusually good or successful. ---
examples: It was a banner year for the company.
Farmers had a banner harvest.
The Braves are coming off a banner season.
entries.contrast: Only before a noun, mostly a banner year or a banner season. The noun banner is a flag or a long sign.

entries.meaning: Having gone through the Christian ceremony of baptism. ---
examples: She's a baptized Catholic.
Only baptized members can take communion.
He was raised in the church but was never baptized.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Barbados. ---
examples: Rihanna is Barbadian.
Barbadian rum is famous around the world.
They flew the Barbadian flag at the festival.
entries.contrast: The informal word is Bajan.

entries.meaning: Extremely cruel and violent. ---
examples: Many people think the death penalty is barbaric.
It was a barbaric attack on civilians.
Conditions in the prison were even more barbaric than reported.

entries.meaning: Cooked slowly over a fire or on a grill, often with a sauce. ---
examples: We had barbecued ribs for dinner.
The chicken is barbecued over charcoal.
They sell barbecued corn at the fair.

entries.meaning: Barbed has 2 distinct senses.

She made a barbed comment about his weight.
His jokes got more barbed as the night went on.

senses.head: Having sharp points that stick out backward
examples: The farm is surrounded by a barbed wire fence.
The hook is barbed so the fish can't get off.

senses.head: Meant to hurt someone's feelings
examples: She made a barbed comment about his weight.
His jokes got more barbed as the night went on.

entries.meaning: Bare has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Don't walk on the hot sand in bare feet.
The trees were bare by November.
He slept on the bare floor.
Store shelves were bare before the hurricane.
The apartment still had bare walls.
We packed only the bare necessities.
He did the bare minimum to pass.
There wasn't even the barest hint of a smile.

senses.head: Not covered by clothes or anything else
examples: Don't walk on the hot sand in bare feet.
The trees were bare by November.
He slept on the bare floor.

senses.head: Empty; without the usual things
examples: Store shelves were bare before the hurricane.
The apartment still had bare walls.

senses.head: Only the most basic; the smallest amount needed
examples: We packed only the bare necessities.
He did the bare minimum to pass.
There wasn't even the barest hint of a smile.

entries.position: both — before a noun only in the sense 'the smallest amount'
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like bear. For 'naked' about a whole person Americans usually say naked; bare is for parts of the body and surfaces.

entries.meaning: Bare-knuckle has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Bare-knuckle boxing is legal in some states.
The two men got into a bare-knuckle fight outside the bar.
It was a bare-knuckle political campaign.
The firm is known for bare-knuckle business tactics.

senses.head: Fought with fists and no boxing gloves
examples: Bare-knuckle boxing is legal in some states.
The two men got into a bare-knuckle fight outside the bar.

senses.head: Aggressive and without any rules or restraint
examples: It was a bare-knuckle political campaign.
The firm is known for bare-knuckle business tactics.

entries.meaning: Riding a horse without a saddle. ---
examples: Bareback riding is one of the toughest rodeo events.
The circus had a bareback rider in a sparkly costume.
The ranch offers bareback lessons for experienced riders.
entries.contrast: More often an adverb: She rode bareback.

entries.meaning: Not wearing shoes or socks. ---
examples: She was barefoot when she answered the door.
Two barefoot kids were playing in the yard.
Is it OK to go barefoot in here?
entries.contrast: Also an adverb (walk barefoot), with the same form. Barefooted exists but is less common.

entries.meaning: Relating to air pressure or a barometer. ---
examples: Barometric pressure drops before a storm.

entries.meaning: Baroque has 2 distinct senses.

The tax rules are baroque.
His writing is even more baroque than his speeches.

senses.head: In the style of European art, buildings and music of about 1600 to 1750
examples: We went to a concert of baroque music.
The church has a painted baroque ceiling.

senses.head: Too complicated or full of decoration
examples: The tax rules are baroque.
His writing is even more baroque than his speeches.

entries.contrast: For the historical style it is often written with a capital: Baroque music.

senses.head: Having bars across it
examples: The house has barred windows.

senses.head: Not allowed to do something or go somewhere
examples: He is barred from entering the country.

entries.meaning: Barren has 2 distinct senses.

The hills looked even more barren in winter.

senses.head: Producing no results or useful ideas
examples: It was a barren period in her career.
The talks were barren of progress.

entries.contrast: Barren for a woman who cannot have children is old-fashioned and now sounds offensive.

entries.meaning: Blocked or shut in behind a barrier. ---
examples: Police surrounded the barricaded house.

entries.meaning: Base has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Morally low; without honor
examples: The ad appeals to people's basest instincts.
Greed is one of the baser human emotions.
He was driven by base motives.

senses.head: Of a metal: common and not valuable
examples: Alchemists tried to turn base metals into gold.
The ring is a base metal with gold plating.

entries.contrast: Formal. Base is far more often a noun (a military base) or a verb (based on).

entries.meaning: Based has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Having its main office or home in a place

She works for a Denver-based startup.
Where are you based?

senses.head: Using something as the starting point or source
examples: The movie is based on a true story.
Her decision was based on the facts.

entries.position: predicative only — before a noun only in compounds: a Denver-based company
entries.takes: in or at + place; on + source
entries.contrast: ✗ basing on the numbers → based on the numbers.

entries.meaning: Not supported by any facts. ---

entries.meaning: Shy and easily embarrassed. ---

senses.head: Forming the main or most necessary part

senses.head: Simple, with nothing extra
examples: The hotel room was pretty basic.
I only know some basic Spanish.
This is the most basic model they sell.

senses.head: Ordinary and unoriginal, following popular trends (slang)
examples: Pumpkin spice lattes? That's so basic.

senses.head: Hurt by repeated violence
examples: The shelter helps battered women and their children.
The battered boxer could barely stand.

senses.head: Covered in batter and fried

entries.meaning: Getting its power from a battery. ---
examples: I bought a battery-powered lawn mower.

entries.meaning: Damaged or marked by fighting or long struggle. ---

entries.meaning: Slightly crazy or strange in a harmless way. ---

entries.meaning: Of or from Bavaria, a state in southern Germany. ---

Her grandparents were Bavarian.

examples: She wore a beaded dress to the wedding.
Her moccasins are beaded and fringed.

senses.head: Covered with small drops of liquid
examples: His forehead was beaded with sweat.
The cold glass was beaded with water.

entries.meaning: (Of eyes) small, round and shiny, often in a way that seems unfriendly or greedy. ---

entries.meaning: Smiling widely because very happy. ---
examples: The beaming parents posed with their son at graduation.

entries.meaning: Possible to accept or deal with, though unpleasant. ---
examples: The heat was bearable once the sun went down.

entries.meaning: Having a beard. ---

entries.meaning: Bearish has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Expecting prices on a financial market to fall
examples: Many analysts are bearish on oil right now.
The market has been bearish for months.
Investors grew more bearish after the jobs report.

senses.head: Big, heavy and a little rough, like a bear
examples: He gave me a bearish hug.
Her dad is a bearish guy with a surprisingly soft voice.

entries.meaning: Old and in bad condition from a lot of use. ---

entries.meaning: Beaten has 3 distinct senses.

We followed a beaten path through the woods.
The best restaurants are off the beaten path.
Add two beaten eggs to the flour.
Brush the dough with beaten egg before baking.

senses.head: Defeated, and feeling that you have lost
examples: The beaten team walked slowly off the field.
After the third rejection he felt beaten.

senses.head: (Of a path) worn flat by many people walking on it
examples: We followed a beaten path through the woods.
The best restaurants are off the beaten path.

senses.head: (Of eggs or cream) mixed quickly until smooth
examples: Add two beaten eggs to the flour.
Brush the dough with beaten egg before baking.

entries.position: both — a beaten team, He looked beaten

entries.meaning: Beautiful has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Very attractive to look at
examples: She has a beautiful smile.
The view from the top is beautiful.
It's the most beautiful beach I've ever seen.

senses.head: Very pleasant or good; done very well
examples: What a beautiful day!
That was a beautiful pass.
She's a beautiful person, inside and out.

entries.meaning: (Of clothes or a hairstyle) making someone look attractive. ---

entries.meaning: Wet, dirty and messy. ---

He got a lot beefier after a year at the gym.

senses.head: Bigger or more powerful than usual

entries.meaning: Suitable for a particular person or occasion. ---

entries.meaning: Confused and unable to think clearly. ---
examples: A befuddled tourist asked us for directions.

entries.meaning: At the first level; for people just starting to learn something. ---

This series is for beginning readers.
The class is full of beginning guitar players.
entries.contrast: A beginning student is American; British English prefers a beginner or a beginners' class. The beginning on its own is the noun.

entries.meaning: Charming and attractive, sometimes in a way that misleads. ---

The idea is beguiling, but it won't work in practice.
It's one of the most beguiling novels of the year.

entries.meaning: Connected with how people or animals behave. ---
examples: The school hired a behavioral specialist.
Behavioral therapy helped him with his anxiety.
Scientists studied behavioral changes in the mice.
entries.contrast: American spelling; British English writes behavioural.

entries.meaning: Behind has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We're two weeks behind on the project.
They fell behind on the rent after he lost his job.
The flight put us behind schedule.
The Cubs were behind by three runs in the seventh.
She's still behind in the polls, but the gap is closing.

senses.head: Late with work, payments or a schedule
examples: We're two weeks behind on the project.
They fell behind on the rent after he lost his job.
The flight put us behind schedule.

senses.head: Losing in a game or a contest
examples: The Cubs were behind by three runs in the seventh.
She's still behind in the polls, but the gap is closing.

entries.position: predicative only — we're behind, never a behind student
entries.comparison: not gradable — but far behind, further behind
entries.takes: on, with or in + noun; by + amount
entries.contrast: Behind is much more often a preposition (behind the house) or an adverb (stay behind). Only the 'late' and 'losing' uses after be or get are adjectival.

entries.meaning: Happening in private, out of public view. ---
examples: The DVD includes a behind-the-scenes look at the movie.
There was a lot of behind-the-scenes negotiating before the deal.
Her behind-the-scenes work kept the campaign running.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb it has no hyphens: work behind the scenes

entries.meaning: Owing something to someone, so that you must do what they want. ---
examples: The senator is beholden to big donors.
I don't want to be beholden to anyone.
Local papers were beholden to their advertisers.

entries.meaning: Of or from Belarus, its people or its language. ---
examples: She's a Belarusian tennis player.
Belarusian and Russian are both official languages there.
His parents are Belarusian.
entries.contrast: The older spelling Byelorussian is dated. Also a noun for the person and the language.

entries.meaning: Coming or happening later than it should. ---
examples: Happy belated birthday!
I sent her a belated thank-you note.
His apology was sincere but belated.

entries.meaning: Of or from Belgium. ---
examples: We had Belgian waffles for breakfast.
Is this chocolate Belgian?
The Belgian rider won the race.

entries.meaning: Easy to believe; seeming real. ---
examples: The characters in the show are very believable.
He needed a believable excuse for being late.
Her second version of the story was more believable.
entries.contrast: In everyday talk unbelievable usually means 'amazing' (The game was unbelievable!); believable only means 'realistic, easy to believe'.

entries.meaning: Making someone or something seem unimportant. ---
examples: Her boss made belittling comments about her work.
His tone was belittling.
It was the most belittling thing anyone had ever said to me.

entries.meaning: (Of pants) very wide at the bottom of the legs. ---
examples: She found a pair of bell-bottom jeans at a thrift store.
Bell-bottom pants were everywhere in the 1970s.
The sailors wore white bell-bottom trousers.
entries.form: compound — bell + bottom; the pants themselves are bell-bottoms

entries.meaning: Shaped like a bell, narrow at the top and wide at the bottom. ---
examples: Test scores usually fall on a bell-shaped curve.
The plant has small bell-shaped flowers.
The lampshade is bell-shaped.

entries.meaning: Eager to fight or start a war. ---
examples: The general's bellicose speech worried the neighboring countries.
The president's tone has become more bellicose.
He gets bellicose when he drinks.

entries.meaning: Belligerent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The belligerent customer was asked to leave.
He got belligerent when the police arrived.
Her emails grew more belligerent every week.
The belligerent nations agreed to a ceasefire.
Neither of the belligerent sides would give up the city.

senses.head: Angry and ready to argue or fight
examples: The belligerent customer was asked to leave.
He got belligerent when the police arrived.
Her emails grew more belligerent every week.

senses.head: (Formal, of a country or group) fighting in a war
examples: The belligerent nations agreed to a ceasefire.
Neither of the belligerent sides would give up the city.

entries.meaning: (Of a business) failed or bankrupt. ---
examples: The restaurant went belly-up after a year.
Half the startups in that building have gone belly-up.
If sales don't improve, we'll be belly-up by summer.
entries.position: predicative only — almost always go belly-up
entries.form: compound — belly + up, like a dead fish floating upside down

entries.meaning: Loved very much. ---
examples: He was a beloved teacher at the school for thirty years.
The park is beloved by locals.
She's one of the most beloved singers in the country.

entries.meaning: Unfair and hurtful. ---
examples: That comment about his divorce was below the belt.
Bringing up her weight was a little below the belt.
The ad was a below-the-belt attack on his family.
entries.position: both — That was below the belt; hyphenated before a noun: a below-the-belt joke
entries.comparison: not gradable — though a little below the belt is common
entries.form: idiom — from boxing, where hitting below the belt is against the rules

entries.meaning: Bemused has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He looked bemused by all the questions.
She gave me a bemused look when I answered in French.
He watched the kids' argument with a bemused smile.
She read the angry comments with bemused detachment.

senses.head: Puzzled and a little confused
examples: He looked bemused by all the questions.
She gave me a bemused look when I answered in French.

senses.head: Mildly amused, often because something seems odd
examples: He watched the kids' argument with a bemused smile.
She read the angry comments with bemused detachment.

entries.contrast: A trap: bemused traditionally means 'puzzled', not 'amused'. Many Americans now use it for 'mildly amused', so context decides; careful writers keep it for 'puzzled'.

entries.meaning: Easy to bend without breaking. ---
examples: The toy has bendable arms and legs.
Give the kids bendable straws.
This wire is more bendable than the old kind.

entries.meaning: Having a good effect; helpful. ---
examples: Regular exercise is beneficial to your health.
The deal was beneficial for both companies.
Some bacteria are actually beneficial.

entries.meaning: Benevolent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He ran the company like a benevolent grandfather.
The old king was seen as benevolent.
The benevolent society paid for the funeral.
He left his money to a police benevolent association.

senses.head: Kind and wanting to help others
examples: He ran the company like a benevolent grandfather.
The old king was seen as benevolent.

senses.head: (Of an organization) set up to help people in need
examples: The benevolent society paid for the funeral.
He left his money to a police benevolent association.

entries.meaning: Of or from Bengal, its people or its language. ---
examples: We ordered Bengali fish curry.
Bengali literature has a long history.
Her family is Bengali.
entries.contrast: Covers both Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal. Also the name of the language and a person: She speaks Bengali.

entries.meaning: Benign has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Luckily, the tumor was benign.
The doctor removed a small benign growth.
Most of these apps are fairly benign.
The side effects are usually benign.
He had a benign smile.
The weather was benign all week.

senses.head: (Of a tumor or growth) not cancerous
examples: Luckily, the tumor was benign.
The doctor removed a small benign growth.

senses.head: Not harmful or dangerous
examples: Most of these apps are fairly benign.
The side effects are usually benign.

senses.head: Kind, gentle or mild
examples: He had a benign smile.
The weather was benign all week.

entries.comparison: more/most — not gradable in the medical sense
entries.contrast: The g is silent: it rhymes with nine.

entries.meaning: Bent has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The nail was bent, so I pulled it out.
Keep your knees bent when you lift the box.
The front wheel of my bike is bent.
An old man, bent with age, shuffled past.
She sat bent over her desk all afternoon.
Don't get all bent out of shape about it.
He got bent out of shape over a parking ticket.

senses.head: No longer straight; curved or folded
examples: The nail was bent, so I pulled it out.
Keep your knees bent when you lift the box.
The front wheel of my bike is bent.

senses.head: (Of a person) bending forward
examples: An old man, bent with age, shuffled past.
She sat bent over her desk all afternoon.

senses.head: (bent out of shape, informal) Upset or angry
examples: Don't get all bent out of shape about it.
He got bent out of shape over a parking ticket.

entries.comparison: more/most — usually slightly bent or badly bent
entries.contrast: Bent on something means 'determined to do it' — see bent on. British slang bent 'dishonest' is not used in American English.

entries.meaning: Determined to do something, often something bad. ---
examples: He seems bent on ruining my weekend.
The team came out bent on revenge.
She's bent on becoming a pilot.
entries.position: predicative only — also directly after a noun: a man bent on revenge
entries.comparison: not gradable — hell-bent on is the strong form

entries.meaning: Having lost a close relative or friend who has died. ---
examples: The bereaved family asked for privacy.
Counselors are available for bereaved parents.
She was recently bereaved and still in shock.
entries.contrast: The bereaved is used as a noun for the people whose relative has died. Compare bereft, which is about a feeling of loss or lack.

entries.meaning: Bereft has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The team seemed bereft of ideas.
The town was bereft of jobs after the plant closed.
She was bereft after her husband died.
The kids felt bereft when their best friend moved away.

senses.head: Completely without something
examples: The team seemed bereft of ideas.
The town was bereft of jobs after the plant closed.

senses.head: Very sad and lonely because someone has died or left
examples: She was bereft after her husband died.
The kids felt bereft when their best friend moved away.

entries.position: predicative only — a bereft mother is rare

entries.meaning: Wildly out of control, with anger or excitement. ---
examples: The crowd went berserk when the band came on.
The dog goes berserk whenever the mail carrier comes.
My phone went berserk and started calling people.
entries.position: predicative only — almost always go berserk

entries.meaning: Besieged has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Food was running out in the besieged city.
The besieged soldiers held out for six months.
The besieged star hid from photographers.
Teachers say they feel besieged by new rules.

senses.head: Surrounded by an army that is trying to capture it
examples: Food was running out in the besieged city.
The besieged soldiers held out for six months.

senses.head: Overwhelmed by many people, questions or requests
examples: The besieged star hid from photographers.
Teachers say they feel besieged by new rules.

entries.meaning: So in love with someone or something that you cannot think clearly. ---
examples: He's completely besotted with his new girlfriend.
The besotted grandparents took hundreds of photos.
She's besotted with that puppy.

entries.meaning: Wearing glasses. ---
examples: A bespectacled librarian helped us find the book.
The suspect was described as tall and bespectacled.
The bespectacled professor peered over his notes.

entries.meaning: Made specially for one customer. ---
examples: He paid $5,000 for a bespoke suit.
The agency builds bespoke software for banks.
Every piece of furniture in the hotel is bespoke.
entries.contrast: Originally British. Americans usually say custom or custom-made; bespoke sounds upscale and shows up in marketing (bespoke software, bespoke cocktails).

entries.meaning: Known by the most people. ---
examples: It's her best-known novel.
He's best known for his role in a TV comedy.
The best-known landmark in the city is the bridge.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; best known after a verb
entries.comparison: irregular — the superlative of well-known: well-known, better-known, best-known

entries.meaning: Loved by the most people. ---
examples: It's one of America's best-loved songs.
The bakery's best-loved item is the cinnamon roll.
Of all his books, this one is best loved by kids.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; best loved after a verb
entries.comparison: irregular — the superlative of well-loved: well-loved, best-loved

entries.meaning: Selling in very large numbers. ---
examples: She's a best-selling author with over twenty novels.
It was the best-selling car in America last year.
The album became their best-selling record.
entries.comparison: not gradable — best is already built in
entries.form: compound — best + selling; also written bestselling
entries.contrast: A best-selling author usually just means 'very popular, on the bestseller list', not literally number one.

entries.meaning: Better off has 2 distinct senses.
examples: You'd be better off taking the train.
She's better off without him.
We'd have been best off staying home.
Most families are better off than they were ten years ago.
The better-off neighborhoods are on the north side.

senses.head: In a better situation
examples: You'd be better off taking the train.
She's better off without him.
We'd have been best off staying home.

senses.head: Having more money
examples: Most families are better off than they were ten years ago.
The better-off neighborhoods are on the north side.

entries.position: both — mostly after a verb; hyphenated before a noun: better-off families
entries.comparison: irregular — the comparative of well off: well off, better off, best off
entries.contrast: You'd be better off + -ing is a common way to give advice: You'd be better off calling first.

entries.meaning: Known by more people. ---
examples: He's better known as a singer than as an actor.
The better-known brands cost twice as much.
Samuel Clemens, better known as Mark Twain, grew up in Missouri.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; better known after a verb
entries.comparison: irregular — the comparative of well-known: well-known, better-known, best-known
entries.contrast: Better known as introduces the more familiar name: Samuel Clemens, better known as Mark Twain.

entries.meaning: More attractive to look at. ---
examples: He's much better-looking in person.
The new phone is better-looking than the old one.
She married the best-looking guy in her class.
entries.comparison: irregular — the comparative of good-looking: good-looking, better-looking, best-looking

entries.meaning: Very confused and not sure what to do. ---
examples: A bewildered tourist stood in the middle of the station.
I was bewildered by all the forms.
She looked even more bewildered after his explanation.
entries.contrast: Bewildered is how you feel; bewildering is what causes the feeling: a bewildering choice of cereals.

entries.meaning: Bewitched has 2 distinct senses.
examples: In the story, the prince lives in a bewitched castle.
The villagers believed the well was bewitched.
He was completely bewitched by her voice.
Bewitched audiences stayed until the last song.

senses.head: Under a magic spell
examples: In the story, the prince lives in a bewitched castle.
The villagers believed the well was bewitched.

senses.head: Strongly attracted or charmed
examples: He was completely bewitched by her voice.
Bewitched audiences stayed until the last song.

entries.comparison: more/most — not gradable in the magic sense

entries.meaning: So beautiful or charming that you cannot stop looking or listening. ---
examples: She had bewitching green eyes.
The music was strange and bewitching.
It's the most bewitching place I've ever visited.

entries.meaning: Certain; impossible to question. ---
examples: Her talent is beyond doubt.
The facts of the case are now beyond doubt.
His loyalty to the team was never beyond doubt.
entries.contrast: Also an adverb phrase after verbs: proved beyond doubt. The American legal standard is beyond a reasonable doubt.

entries.meaning: Of or from Bhutan. ---
examples: Bhutanese food is famous for its chili peppers.
The Bhutanese government measures 'Gross National Happiness'.
Many families in the neighborhood are Bhutanese.

entries.meaning: Happening twice a year. ---
examples: The store's biannual sale is in January and July.
Don't forget your biannual dental checkup.
The board holds biannual meetings in spring and fall.
entries.contrast: Easy to confuse with biennial (every two years). Biannual means twice a year; twice-yearly is clearer.

entries.meaning: Unfairly favoring one side. ---
examples: The referee was clearly biased against our team.
Many viewers think the coverage is biased.
The survey questions were biased toward younger people.
entries.takes: against, toward or in favor of + noun

entries.meaning: Biblical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The movie tells a biblical story.
The name Noah is biblical.
The city faced a traffic jam of biblical proportions.
The flooding this spring was biblical.

senses.head: Relating to or found in the Bible
examples: The movie tells a biblical story.
The name Noah is biblical.

senses.head: Very large or extreme, like events in the Bible
examples: The city faced a traffic jam of biblical proportions.
The flooding this spring was biblical.

entries.meaning: Relating to lists of books and articles. ---
examples: The book ends with a long bibliographical note.
Check the bibliographical details before you submit the paper.
The library keeps bibliographical records for every item.

entries.meaning: (Of a lawmaking body) having two parts, or houses. ---
examples: The US Congress is a bicameral legislature.
Nebraska is the only state whose legislature is not bicameral.
Most large democracies have bicameral parliaments.

entries.meaning: Marking two hundred years since something happened. ---
examples: The town held a bicentennial parade.
My parents still have a bicentennial quarter from 1976.
The university is planning its bicentennial celebration.
entries.contrast: American English; British English prefers bicentenary. Also a noun: the nation's bicentennial in 1976.

entries.meaning: Biennial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The art show is a biennial event.
The biennial conference will meet again in 2028.
Parsley is a biennial plant.
Biennial flowers bloom only in their second year.

senses.head: Happening every two years
examples: The art show is a biennial event.
The biennial conference will meet again in 2028.

senses.head: (Of a plant) living for two years
examples: Parsley is a biennial plant.
Biennial flowers bloom only in their second year.

entries.русский: проходящий раз в два года; двулетний
entries.contrast: Biennial is every two years; biannual is twice a year.

entries.meaning: Having a large, heavy body frame. ---
examples: He's a big-boned farm kid from Iowa.
I'm not fat, I'm just big-boned!
The breed is tall and big-boned.
entries.contrast: Often a gentle or joking way to avoid saying 'overweight'.

entries.meaning: Expensive. ---
examples: Families are putting off big-ticket purchases like cars.
Refrigerators and TVs are big-ticket items.
The big-ticket projects were cut from the budget.

entries.meaning: Having strong, unfair opinions about people of another race, religion or group. ---
examples: He made a bigoted comment about immigrants.
Her uncle's views are openly bigoted.
It was the most bigoted speech I've ever heard.

entries.meaning: Bilateral has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The two countries signed a bilateral trade agreement.
Bilateral talks will continue next week.
She had bilateral knee surgery.
The hearing loss is bilateral.

senses.head: Between two countries or groups
examples: The two countries signed a bilateral trade agreement.
Bilateral talks will continue next week.

senses.head: (Medical) on both sides of the body
examples: She had bilateral knee surgery.
The hearing loss is bilateral.

entries.meaning: Speaking two languages well, or using two languages. ---
examples: Their kids are bilingual in English and Spanish.
The school offers bilingual classes.
Road signs in the area are bilingual.

entries.meaning: Rising or spreading out in large waves or clouds. ---
examples: Billowing smoke rose from the warehouse.
She wore a white dress with billowing sleeves.
We watched the billowing storm clouds roll in.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb it is the verb billow: smoke was billowing

entries.meaning: Bimonthly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The newsletter is bimonthly.
We get a bimonthly water bill.
The club holds bimonthly meetings on the first and third Tuesdays.
The bimonthly farmers market runs on the 1st and the 15th.

senses.head: Happening every two months
examples: The newsletter is bimonthly.
We get a bimonthly water bill.

senses.head: Happening twice a month
examples: The club holds bimonthly meetings on the first and third Tuesdays.
The bimonthly farmers market runs on the 1st and the 15th.

entries.русский: выходящий раз в два месяца; дважды в месяц
entries.contrast: Ambiguous: usually 'every two months', but sometimes 'twice a month'. Every other month or twice a month (semimonthly) is clearer. Also an adverb: The magazine comes out bimonthly.

entries.meaning: Binary has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Computers store data in binary code.
Write the number 5 in binary form.
Life isn't a binary choice between success and failure.
Many people reject a binary view of gender.

senses.head: Using only the digits 0 and 1
examples: Computers store data in binary code.
Write the number 5 in binary form.

senses.head: Having only two parts or two options
examples: Life isn't a binary choice between success and failure.
Many people reject a binary view of gender.

entries.meaning: (Of an agreement or decision) that must be obeyed by law. ---
examples: The contract is legally binding.
The decision is binding on both parties.
They signed a binding agreement.
entries.contrast: The binding (noun) is the cover and spine of a book, or the part of a ski that holds the boot.

entries.meaning: Relating to the chemical processes in living things. ---
examples: Stress causes biochemical changes in the brain.
She works in a biochemical research lab.
The test measures biochemical markers in the blood.

entries.meaning: Able to break down naturally and not harm the environment. ---
examples: The cups are made of biodegradable plastic.
Is this packaging biodegradable?
Paper bags are biodegradable, but they still take energy to make.

entries.meaning: About the facts of a person's life. ---
examples: The movie is a biographical drama about a jazz singer.
The website has a short biographical note on each author.
Please include some biographical information with your application.

entries.meaning: Biological has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Sleep is a basic biological need.
The causes of the disease are partly biological.
She found her biological mother at age thirty.
He's not my biological dad, but he raised me.
The treaty bans biological weapons.
Officials trained for a possible biological attack.

senses.head: Relating to living things or to biology
examples: Sleep is a basic biological need.
The causes of the disease are partly biological.

senses.head: Related by birth, not by adoption or marriage
examples: She found her biological mother at age thirty.
He's not my biological dad, but he raised me.

senses.head: (Of weapons) using germs to cause disease
examples: The treaty bans biological weapons.
Officials trained for a possible biological attack.

entries.contrast: For parents, biological is the neutral word; real mother can hurt adoptive families. Russian родной is wider: родной язык is native language, not biological.

entries.meaning: Relating to both biology and medicine. ---
examples: He studied biomedical engineering.
The company makes biomedical devices like pacemakers.
The grant funds biomedical research on cancer.

entries.meaning: Bionic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The veteran walks on a bionic leg.
Researchers are testing a bionic eye.
Our goalie has bionic reflexes.
She must have bionic hearing — she heard us from upstairs.

senses.head: Having or being electronic body parts
examples: The veteran walks on a bionic leg.
Researchers are testing a bionic eye.

senses.head: (Informal) Stronger or better than a normal person
examples: Our goalie has bionic reflexes.
She must have bionic hearing — she heard us from upstairs.

entries.meaning: Supported by or involving both main political parties. ---
examples: The bill passed with bipartisan support.
A bipartisan group of senators wrote the plan.
Voters want a more bipartisan approach.
entries.contrast: A key word in US politics: supported by both Democrats and Republicans.

entries.meaning: Bipolar has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her brother was diagnosed with bipolar disorder.
He's bipolar and takes medication for it.
The bipolar world of the Cold War ended in 1991.
Scientists studied the star's bipolar jets of gas.

senses.head: Having bipolar disorder, a mental illness with extreme changes of mood
examples: Her brother was diagnosed with bipolar disorder.
He's bipolar and takes medication for it.

senses.head: Having two opposite poles or two main powers
examples: The bipolar world of the Cold War ended in 1991.
Scientists studied the star's bipolar jets of gas.

entries.contrast: Using bipolar casually for 'moody' (the weather is so bipolar) is common but offends many people.

entries.meaning: Having parents of two different races. ---
examples: She's biracial — her mom is Korean and her dad is Black.
The show follows a biracial family in Atlanta.
Many biracial Americans check more than one box on the census.

entries.meaning: Sexually attracted to more than one gender. ---
examples: He came out as bisexual in college.
The novel has a bisexual main character.
The group supports gay, lesbian and bisexual teens.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (a bisexual), but the adjective is more usual; bi is the informal short form.

entries.meaning: Mean and unkind in what you say about people. ---
examples: She made a bitchy remark about my hair.
Sorry I was so bitchy this morning.
The comments got bitchier as the night went on.
entries.contrast: Rude slang, mostly about women; avoid it in polite or professional speech.

entries.meaning: Biting has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We walked home in the biting wind.
The cold that morning was biting.
The critic wrote a biting review.
Her humor is more biting than her sister's.

senses.head: (Of wind or cold) so cold that it hurts
examples: We walked home in the biting wind.
The cold that morning was biting.

senses.head: (Of words) sharp and cruel
examples: The critic wrote a biting review.
Her humor is more biting than her sister's.

entries.meaning: Bitter has 5 distinct senses.
examples: This coffee is too bitter for me.
The longer the tea steeps, the more bitter it gets.
He's still bitter about losing his job.
She gave a short, bitter laugh.
The loss was a bitter disappointment.
She learned from bitter experience not to trust him.
The two brothers became bitter enemies.
It was the bitterest election fight in years.
A bitter wind blew off the lake.
Chicago had its bitterest winter in decades.

senses.head: Having a strong, sharp taste that is not sweet
examples: This coffee is too bitter for me.
The longer the tea steeps, the more bitter it gets.

senses.head: Angry and upset because you think you were treated unfairly
examples: He's still bitter about losing his job.
She gave a short, bitter laugh.

senses.head: Making you very unhappy; hard to accept
examples: The loss was a bitter disappointment.
She learned from bitter experience not to trust him.

senses.head: Full of hate; very intense
examples: The two brothers became bitter enemies.
It was the bitterest election fight in years.

senses.head: (Of weather) extremely cold
examples: A bitter wind blew off the lake.
Chicago had its bitterest winter in decades.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — bitterer or more bitter, bitterest
entries.contrast: Russian горький перец is hot pepper in English: bitter is the taste of coffee, dark chocolate or medicine, never spicy heat.

entries.meaning: Bittersweet has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Graduation was a bittersweet day for her.
The ending of the movie is bittersweet.
Melt six ounces of bittersweet chocolate.
I prefer bittersweet chocolate to milk chocolate.

senses.head: Happy and sad at the same time
examples: Graduation was a bittersweet day for her.
The ending of the movie is bittersweet.

senses.head: (Of chocolate) dark and only slightly sweet
examples: Melt six ounces of bittersweet chocolate.
I prefer bittersweet chocolate to milk chocolate.

entries.contrast: In American recipes bittersweet chocolate is dark chocolate with only a little sugar.

entries.meaning: Biweekly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Most of us get a biweekly paycheck.
The team has biweekly planning meetings.
She has biweekly physical therapy, on Tuesdays and Fridays.
The paper went from weekly to biweekly delivery, Mondays and Thursdays.

senses.head: Happening every two weeks
examples: Most of us get a biweekly paycheck.
The team has biweekly planning meetings.

senses.head: Happening twice a week
examples: She has biweekly physical therapy, on Tuesdays and Fridays.
The paper went from weekly to biweekly delivery, Mondays and Thursdays.

entries.русский: раз в две недели; дважды в неделю
entries.contrast: Ambiguous: in the US it usually means 'every two weeks' (a biweekly paycheck), but it can mean 'twice a week'. Every other week or twice a week is clearer. Also an adverb: We get paid biweekly.

entries.meaning: Very strange and unusual. ---
examples: I had a bizarre dream last night.
His behavior at the party was bizarre.
It's the most bizarre story I've heard all year.
entries.contrast: Sounds almost like bazaar (a market), but means 'very strange'.

entries.meaning: Covered in bruises. ---
examples: His arm was black and blue after the fall.
She showed me her black-and-blue knee.
The older kids beat him black and blue.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; black and blue after a verb

entries.meaning: Black-and-white has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Grandpa watched black-and-white TV as a kid.
The old photos are all black and white.
Life isn't as black and white as you think.
He has a very black-and-white view of the world.

senses.head: Showing only black, white and gray, with no other colors
examples: Grandpa watched black-and-white TV as a kid.
The old photos are all black and white.

senses.head: Seeing things as simply right or wrong, with nothing in between
examples: Life isn't as black and white as you think.
He has a very black-and-white view of the world.

entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; black and white after a verb
entries.comparison: not gradable — but in the second sense as, so, very are common: not as black and white as it looks
entries.contrast: In black and white (a noun phrase) means 'in writing': It's right there in black and white.

entries.meaning: Bought or sold illegally, outside the legal market. ---
examples: Agents seized thousands of black-market cigarettes.
Black-market prices for the drug tripled last year.
He paid a black-market dealer twice what the ticket was worth.
entries.contrast: The noun is two separate words: goods sold on the black market. Only the adjective before a noun takes the hyphen.

entries.meaning: Requiring formal evening clothes. ---
examples: They're going to a black-tie dinner at the museum.
The gala is black-tie, so rent a tux.
Is the wedding black-tie or casual?
entries.form: compound — black + tie (a bow tie worn with a tuxedo)
entries.contrast: Black-tie means men wear a tuxedo; white-tie is even more formal. On invitations the dress code is written without a hyphen: Black tie optional.

entries.meaning: Blackened has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Firefighters walked through the blackened remains of the house.
The walls of the old kitchen were blackened with soot.
He pulled a blackened pan out of the oven.
I'll have the blackened catfish with rice.
The restaurant is famous for its blackened chicken sandwich.

senses.head: Made black by smoke, fire or dirt
examples: Firefighters walked through the blackened remains of the house.
The walls of the old kitchen were blackened with soot.
He pulled a blackened pan out of the oven.

senses.head: Of food, coated in spices and cooked quickly in a very hot pan until dark, in the Cajun style
examples: I'll have the blackened catfish with rice.
The restaurant is famous for its blackened chicken sandwich.

entries.position: both — the cooking sense only before a noun

entries.meaning: Not responsible for anything bad; having done nothing wrong. ---
examples: The report found that the driver was blameless.
Neither side in the divorce was completely blameless.
She had lived a quiet, blameless life.

entries.meaning: Bland has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The soup was a little bland, so I added some salt.
After the surgery he had to stick to a bland diet.
This is the blandest salsa I've ever tasted.
The office was painted a bland beige.
The senator gave a bland statement that said almost nothing.

senses.head: Of food, having very little flavor
examples: The soup was a little bland, so I added some salt.
After the surgery he had to stick to a bland diet.
This is the blandest salsa I've ever tasted.

senses.head: Dull and uninteresting; without strong features or opinions
examples: The office was painted a bland beige.
The senator gave a bland statement that said almost nothing.

entries.meaning: Blank has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Write your answer on a blank sheet of paper.
Please don't leave any lines blank.
The screen suddenly went blank.
When I asked about the money, he just gave me a blank look.
As soon as the test started, my mind went blank.

senses.head: With nothing written, printed or recorded on it
examples: Write your answer on a blank sheet of paper.
Please don't leave any lines blank.
The screen suddenly went blank.

senses.head: Showing no expression, understanding or memory
examples: When I asked about the money, he just gave me a blank look.
As soon as the test started, my mind went blank.

entries.contrast: The noun is common too: fill in the blanks, my mind drew a blank. A blank check is a signed check with no amount, and figuratively unlimited freedom.

entries.meaning: Applying to all cases or people, without exceptions. ---
examples: The city imposed a blanket ban on fireworks.
That's a blanket statement, and it isn't fair to everyone.
The policy offers blanket coverage for all employees.
entries.position: attributive only — a blanket ban, never the ban was blanket
entries.contrast: Much more often a noun (одеяло). As an adjective it only comes before a noun and means applying to everything, with no exceptions — often with disapproval: a blanket statement.

entries.meaning: Making a very loud, harsh noise. ---
examples: We could hear blaring sirens all night.
He drove past with his music blaring.
The TV in the waiting room was blaring.

entries.meaning: Not impressed or worried by something, often because you have seen it many times before. ---
examples: New Yorkers are pretty blase about celebrities on the subway.
She sounded blase, but I could tell she was nervous.
The second time around, I was a lot more blase about flying.

entries.meaning: Showing disrespect for God or for something religious; humorously, disrespecting something people treat as sacred. ---
examples: The film was banned in several countries as blasphemous.
Some viewers found the painting blasphemous.
In Chicago, putting ketchup on a hot dog is about the most blasphemous thing you can do.
entries.contrast: The stress moves: the adjective and the noun are BLAS-fuh-, but the verb blaspheme is blas-FEEM.

entries.meaning: Very obvious and done openly, without shame. ---
examples: That was a blatant lie, and everyone in the room knew it.
The referee missed a blatant foul.
It was the most blatant case of discrimination the lawyer had ever seen.
entries.contrast: Blatant is about something bad done openly, without trying to hide it: a blatant lie. For something simply easy to see, use obvious.

entries.meaning: Blazing has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We sat around a blazing campfire.
The players were exhausted after two hours in the blazing sun.
It was a blazing July afternoon in Phoenix.
The new phone runs at blazing speed.
He ran the forty-yard dash in a blazing 4.3 seconds.

senses.head: Burning strongly and brightly; of the sun or weather, extremely hot
examples: We sat around a blazing campfire.
The players were exhausted after two hours in the blazing sun.
It was a blazing July afternoon in Phoenix.

senses.head: Extremely fast
examples: The new phone runs at blazing speed.
He ran the forty-yard dash in a blazing 4.3 seconds.

entries.contrast: The fire was blazing is usually the verb blaze. Before another adjective, blazing works like an adverb: blazing hot, blazing fast.

entries.meaning: Made white or lighter in color by chemicals or by the sun. ---
examples: She showed up with bleached blond hair.
The old fence was bleached by years of desert sun.
Some bakers prefer unbleached flour to bleached flour.

entries.meaning: Bleak has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The future looks bleak for the town's last factory.
Doctors gave him a bleak prognosis.
Things got even bleaker when the funding ran out.
The prairie looks bleak in the middle of winter.
It was a gray, bleak February morning.

senses.head: Without hope or encouragement
examples: The future looks bleak for the town's last factory.
Doctors gave him a bleak prognosis.
Things got even bleaker when the funding ran out.

senses.head: Of a place or weather, cold, bare and unwelcoming
examples: The prairie looks bleak in the middle of winter.
It was a gray, bleak February morning.

entries.meaning: Of eyes, tired and unable to see clearly, especially from lack of sleep. ---
examples: He looked at me with bleary eyes and asked what time it was.
My eyes were bleary after staring at the screen all night.
By the end of the flight, the passengers looked even blearier than the crew.

entries.meaning: Having tired, red eyes that cannot see clearly, usually after too little sleep. ---
examples: A few bleary-eyed students showed up for the 8 a.m. class.
She came downstairs bleary-eyed and went straight for the coffee.
We were all bleary-eyed after the overnight drive.

entries.meaning: Blended has 2 distinct senses.
examples: This is a blended whiskey, not a single malt.
The school uses blended learning, with some classes online.
Pour in the blended fruit and stir.
They're a blended family with five kids between them.
Holidays can be complicated in blended families.

senses.head: Made by mixing different kinds or sources together
examples: This is a blended whiskey, not a single malt.
The school uses blended learning, with some classes online.
Pour in the blended fruit and stir.

senses.head: Of a family, made up of a couple and the children from their earlier relationships
body: ((о семье) смешанная, с детьми от прежних браков)
examples: They're a blended family with five kids between them.
Holidays can be complicated in blended families.

entries.meaning: Blessed has 3 distinct senses.
examples: We've been blessed with three healthy kids.
She's blessed with a great singing voice.
I feel very blessed to have friends like you.
The church is dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary.
The pastor quoted the Bible: "It is more blessed to give than to receive."
After a week of storms, the sunshine was a blessed relief.
The kids finally fell asleep, and there was blessed silence.

senses.head: Lucky to have something good; given a talent or advantage. Pronounced BLEST
examples: We've been blessed with three healthy kids.
She's blessed with a great singing voice.
I feel very blessed to have friends like you.

senses.head: Holy; connected with God. Pronounced BLES-id
examples: The church is dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary.
The pastor quoted the Bible: "It is more blessed to give than to receive."

senses.head: Bringing welcome relief or happiness. Pronounced BLES-id
examples: After a week of storms, the sunshine was a blessed relief.
The kids finally fell asleep, and there was blessed silence.

entries.position: both — blessed with after a verb; a blessed relief before a noun
entries.contrast: The pronunciation follows the meaning. After a verb, lucky is one syllable: We're blessed (BLEST). Before a noun, holy and welcome are two: the Blessed Virgin, a blessed relief (BLES-id).

entries.meaning: Blighted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The program helps rebuild blighted neighborhoods.
The old mill district was one of the most blighted parts of the city.
Rows of blighted houses stood empty along the street.
Farmers had to pull up the blighted potato plants.
His career was blighted by injuries.

senses.head: Of a city area, run-down, neglected and poor
examples: The program helps rebuild blighted neighborhoods.
The old mill district was one of the most blighted parts of the city.
Rows of blighted houses stood empty along the street.

senses.head: Damaged by disease, or spoiled by something bad
examples: Farmers had to pull up the blighted potato plants.
His career was blighted by injuries.

entries.русский: запущенный, пришедший в упадок; поражённый, загубленный

entries.meaning: With a piece of cloth tied over the eyes so that you cannot see. ---
examples: The blindfolded kids took turns swinging at the piñata.
The hostages were kept blindfolded for days.
I've made this drive so many times I could do it blindfolded.

entries.meaning: Blinding has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There was a blinding flash, and then the power went out.
Drivers were stuck in blinding snow on the interstate.
The sun off the water was blinding.
She woke up with a blinding headache.
The car took off at blinding speed.

senses.head: So bright that you cannot see
examples: There was a blinding flash, and then the power went out.
Drivers were stuck in blinding snow on the interstate.
The sun off the water was blinding.

senses.head: Very strong or intense
examples: She woke up with a blinding headache.
The car took off at blinding speed.

entries.meaning: Extremely happy and peaceful. ---
examples: We spent a blissful week on the beach with no phones.
The first months of their marriage were blissful.
It was the most blissful nap of my life.

entries.meaning: Blistering has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The marathon was run in blistering heat.
By noon the sidewalk was blistering.
She set a blistering pace from the start.
The band played a blistering guitar solo.
The paper published a blistering review of the new restaurant.
The senator launched a blistering attack on the plan.

senses.head: Extremely hot
examples: The marathon was run in blistering heat.
By noon the sidewalk was blistering.

senses.head: Very fast
examples: She set a blistering pace from the start.
The band played a blistering guitar solo.

senses.head: Very angry and critical
examples: The paper published a blistering review of the new restaurant.
The senator launched a blistering attack on the plan.

entries.form: -ing from blister, as if hot enough to raise blisters

entries.meaning: Blithe has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The company showed a blithe disregard for safety rules.
He made the blithe assumption that someone else would pay.
She was even more blithe about the deadline than her boss.
She had a blithe spirit that everyone loved.
The song has a blithe, sunny melody.

senses.head: Casual and unconcerned, in a way that seems careless
examples: The company showed a blithe disregard for safety rules.
He made the blithe assumption that someone else would pay.
She was even more blithe about the deadline than her boss.

senses.head: Happy and carefree; mostly in literary writing
examples: She had a blithe spirit that everyone loved.
The song has a blithe, sunny melody.

entries.meaning: With something in the way, so that nothing can get through. ---
examples: The road was blocked by a fallen tree.
He had surgery to open two blocked arteries.
Your number is blocked, so my calls won't go through.
entries.contrast: For a drain or a nose, Americans more often say clogged and stuffy (a clogged drain, a stuffy nose); blocked there sounds more British.

entries.meaning: Deep red, like the color of blood. ---
examples: The sky turned blood-red at sunset.
She wore blood-red lipstick to the premiere.
The moon looked blood-red during the eclipse.

entries.meaning: Extremely frightening, especially of a sound. ---
examples: We heard a bloodcurdling scream from the woods.
The movie has some truly bloodcurdling moments.
The noise from the basement was bloodcurdling.
entries.form: compound — blood + curdling: so frightening it makes your blood go thick

entries.meaning: Bloodless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The government fell in a bloodless coup.
It was a rare bloodless revolution.
His lips were thin and bloodless.
Critics called the remake a bloodless copy of the original.
Her face went bloodless when she heard the news.

senses.head: Done without violence or killing
examples: The government fell in a bloodless coup.
It was a rare bloodless revolution.

senses.head: Very pale; also without energy or emotion
examples: His lips were thin and bloodless.
Critics called the remake a bloodless copy of the original.
Her face went bloodless when she heard the news.

entries.position: both — the violence sense mostly before a noun

entries.meaning: Of eyes, red because the small blood vessels in them are swollen. ---
examples: His eyes were bloodshot from lack of sleep.
She stared at me with bloodshot eyes.
Allergies make my eyes itchy and bloodshot.

entries.meaning: Marked or covered with blood. ---
examples: Police found a bloodstained shirt in the trunk.
The bandage was bloodstained by morning.
The museum displays the general's bloodstained coat.

entries.meaning: Eager to kill or hurt people, or enjoying violence. ---
examples: The story is about a bloodthirsty pirate captain.
The crowd grew bloodthirsty as the fight went on.
It's one of the most bloodthirsty movies of the year.

entries.meaning: Bloody has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He came home from practice with a bloody nose.
Her knees were scraped and bloody.
Someone left a bloody towel on the floor.
Antietam was the bloodiest single day of the Civil War.
The strike ended in a bloody clash with the police.

senses.head: Covered in blood or bleeding
examples: He came home from practice with a bloody nose.
Her knees were scraped and bloody.
Someone left a bloody towel on the floor.

senses.head: Involving a lot of violence and killing
examples: Antietam was the bloodiest single day of the Civil War.
The strike ended in a bloody clash with the police.

entries.contrast: In British English bloody is also a mild swear word used for emphasis (bloody hell). Americans recognize it from British TV but don't use it that way; in American English it means with blood.

entries.meaning: Covered with uneven patches of color, especially red marks on the skin. ---
examples: Her face gets red and blotchy when she cries.
The cheap paint dried blotchy.
The rash was blotchier the next morning.

entries.meaning: Describing every detail of an event in the order it happened. ---
examples: He gave us a blow-by-blow account of the meeting.
The book offers a blow-by-blow history of the campaign.
I don't need a blow-by-blow description, just tell me who won.
entries.form: compound — from a boxing commentary that describes every punch
entries.contrast: After a verb it is an adverb phrase, usually without hyphens: She told us about the fight blow by blow.

entries.meaning: Blue-chip has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her portfolio is mostly blue-chip stocks.
Several blue-chip companies reported strong earnings.
The college landed three blue-chip recruits this year.
The gallery sells blue-chip contemporary art.

senses.head: Of a company or stock, large, well established and reliable
examples: Her portfolio is mostly blue-chip stocks.
Several blue-chip companies reported strong earnings.

senses.head: Of the highest quality, especially of a sports recruit or a work of art
examples: The college landed three blue-chip recruits this year.
The gallery sells blue-chip contemporary art.

entries.form: compound — from the highest-value blue chip in poker

entries.meaning: Doing or connected with physical work in factories, construction and similar jobs. ---
examples: He grew up in a blue-collar town in Ohio.
Many blue-collar jobs now require technical training.
Her family was proudly blue-collar.
entries.form: compound — blue + collar, from work shirts

entries.meaning: Having blue eyes. ---
examples: They have a blue-eyed baby girl.
Both of her sons are blond and blue-eyed.
The poster showed a smiling, blue-eyed soldier.

entries.meaning: Of a color between blue and green. ---
examples: The water in the bay is a clear blue-green.
She bought a blue-green sweater to match her eyes.
The lake turns blue-green in late summer.

entries.meaning: Blue-ribbon has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The governor appointed a blue-ribbon panel to study the problem.

They raise blue-ribbon cattle.

senses.head: Of a group, made up of especially qualified or respected people
examples: The governor appointed a blue-ribbon panel to study the problem.
A blue-ribbon commission released its report on Monday.

senses.head: Of the best quality; having won first prize
examples: Grandma's blue-ribbon apple pie won at the county fair.
They raise blue-ribbon cattle.

entries.form: compound — from the blue ribbon given for first prize

entries.meaning: Slightly blue. ---
examples: The screen gives off a bluish light.
His lips were turning bluish from the cold.
The mountains look bluish in the distance.

entries.meaning: Blunt has 2 distinct senses.
examples: To be blunt, your business plan won't work.
She gave a blunt answer to a simple question.
His feedback was even blunter than I expected.
The victim was hit with a blunt object.
Kids' scissors have blunt tips.

senses.head: Saying exactly what you think, without trying to be polite
examples: To be blunt, your business plan won't work.
She gave a blunt answer to a simple question.
His feedback was even blunter than I expected.

senses.head: Not sharp; having a rounded or flat edge or point
examples: The victim was hit with a blunt object.
Kids' scissors have blunt tips.

entries.contrast: For an everyday knife, Americans usually say dull; blunt is more common in a blunt object and blunt-force trauma.

entries.meaning: Blurred has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Most of the vacation photos came out blurred.
He complained of blurred vision after the fall.
The line between work and home has become blurred.
With remote jobs, those boundaries are more blurred than ever.

senses.head: Not clear in shape or outline
examples: Most of the vacation photos came out blurred.
He complained of blurred vision after the fall.

senses.head: Of a difference or line between things, no longer clear
examples: The line between work and home has become blurred.
With remote jobs, those boundaries are more blurred than ever.

entries.form: -ed from blur, with the r doubled

entries.meaning: Not clear; out of focus. ---
examples: The security footage is too blurry to identify anyone.
Everything looks blurry without my glasses.
This picture is even blurrier than the last one.
entries.form: -y from blur, with the r doubled
entries.contrast: Blurry and blurred mean nearly the same for pictures and eyesight; blurry is the more casual everyday word. Only blurred is used for lines between ideas: blurred boundaries.

entries.meaning: Of weather, with strong, sudden gusts of wind. ---
examples: It was a cold, blustery day in Chicago.
The weekend will be blustery, with gusts up to forty miles an hour.
March was more blustery than usual this year.

entries.meaning: Talking too proudly about yourself and what you have done. ---
examples: He's talented but never boastful.
The coach was annoyed by the team's boastful posts online.
The more he won, the more boastful he became.

entries.meaning: Relating to the human body. ---
examples: He was charged with assault causing bodily harm.
Doctors monitored all of her bodily functions.
Gloves protect nurses from contact with bodily fluids.
entries.form: body + -ly, with y changed to i
entries.contrast: An -ly word that is an adjective, not an adverb. There is also a separate adverb: They carried him bodily out of the bar (by lifting his whole body).

entries.meaning: Fake or false, though pretending to be real; informally, unfair or wrong. ---
examples: The website was selling bogus concert tickets.
Most of his insurance claims turned out to be bogus.
They kicked him out for being late? That's totally bogus.

entries.meaning: Living in an artistic, unconventional way, without caring about ordinary social rules. ---
examples: Greenwich Village was once the center of bohemian life in New York.
Her apartment has a bohemian look, with rugs and plants everywhere.
The neighborhood was a lot more bohemian before the rents went up.
entries.contrast: With a capital letter, Bohemian means from Bohemia, the region of the Czech Republic. Lowercase bohemian (often shortened to boho for fashion) describes an artistic, unconventional lifestyle.

entries.meaning: Cooked in boiling water. ---
examples: I had two boiled eggs for breakfast.
Serve the fish with boiled potatoes.
Are the peanuts roasted or boiled?

entries.meaning: Noisy, energetic and lively. ---
examples: A boisterous crowd filled the stadium.

entries.meaning: Bold has 3 distinct senses.

She likes bold colors like orange and purple.
This coffee has a bold flavor.
The key terms are in bold type.
Put the headings in bold.

senses.head: Brave and confident, willing to take risks; sometimes too confident to be polite
examples: The mayor has a bold plan to rebuild downtown.
It was one of the boldest moves in company history.
If I may be so bold, I think you're making a mistake.

senses.head: Strong, bright and easy to notice
examples: She likes bold colors like orange and purple.
This coffee has a bold flavor.

senses.head: Of printed letters, thick and dark
examples: The key terms are in bold type.
Put the headings in bold.

entries.русский: смелый, дерзкий; яркий, насыщенный; жирный (о шрифте)

entries.meaning: From or connected with Bolivia. ---
examples: La Paz is the seat of the Bolivian government.
My roommate is Bolivian.
We tried Bolivian salteñas at a café in Virginia.
entries.contrast: Always capitalized. A Bolivian, Bolivians are nouns for the people.

entries.meaning: Using loud, grand, impressive-sounding language that has little real meaning. ---
examples: The candidate is known for his bombastic speeches.
Critics found the movie's score loud and bombastic.
Her tweets got more bombastic as the election got closer.

entries.meaning: Bona fide has 2 distinct senses.

Only bona fide residents can get a parking permit.
The company says it made a bona fide offer to the union.
The court decided the sale was bona fide.

senses.head: Real and genuine, not fake or pretending
examples: After one hit song, she became a bona fide star.
Is he a bona fide expert, or does he just play one on TV?
Only bona fide residents can get a parking permit.

senses.head: Made honestly and sincerely, without intending to deceive
examples: The company says it made a bona fide offer to the union.
The court decided the sale was bona fide.

entries.form: Latin for in good faith; two words, no hyphen
entries.contrast: Also said boh-nuh-FY-dee. Do not confuse it with the noun bona fides (proof that someone is qualified or trustworthy): She has the academic bona fides for the job.

entries.meaning: Completely dry, with no water at all. ---
examples: After three months without rain, the creek was bone-dry.
Check that the wood is bone-dry before you paint it.
The turkey came out bone-dry, so we covered it in gravy.
entries.form: compound — bone + dry: as dry as a bone

entries.meaning: Informal: very stupid. ---
examples: Leaving the keys in the car was a boneheaded mistake.
The coach called the penalty boneheaded.
That was the most boneheaded play of the whole season.
entries.form: from the noun bonehead (a stupid person) + -ed

entries.meaning: Of meat or fish, with the bones removed. ---
examples: Buy two pounds of boneless, skinless chicken breasts.
We ordered a dozen boneless wings.
Is the ham boneless?

entries.meaning: Informal: crazy, or wildly excited or angry. ---
examples: You want to drive to Florida tonight? You're bonkers.
The fans went bonkers when the home team scored.
The price of eggs this year is just bonkers.
entries.position: predicative only — he's bonkers, go bonkers
entries.contrast: Informal. It ends in -s but is not a plural: She's bonkers, never ✗ a bonker.

entries.meaning: Bony has 2 distinct senses.

Carp is tasty but very bony.
I don't like bony fish.

senses.head: Very thin, so that the bones show
examples: The stray dog was bony and scared.
He had long, bony fingers.
She was the boniest kid in the class.

senses.head: Of fish, full of small bones
examples: Carp is tasty but very bony.
I don't like bony fish.

entries.meaning: Of a place, event or person, with all the places or time already reserved. ---
examples: Every hotel in town is booked for the game.

Sorry, I'm booked all week, can we meet Monday?
entries.position: predicative only — the hotel is booked
entries.comparison: not gradable — fully booked, booked solid
entries.contrast: He was booked (by the police) is the passive of the verb book, to charge with a crime, not this adjective.

entries.meaning: Liking reading and study more than sports or social activities. ---

entries.meaning: Booming has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Growing quickly and very successful
