Business is booming this summer.
They opened a shop in the town's booming downtown.

senses.head: Of a voice or sound, loud and deep
examples: The announcer has a booming voice.
We heard booming thunder in the distance.

entries.meaning: Rude and rough in behavior; bad-mannered. ---
examples: His boorish behavior at the wedding embarrassed everyone.
The fans in the upper deck were loud and boorish.
He got more boorish with every drink.

entries.meaning: Made, copied or sold illegally. ---

Vendors outside the stadium sell bootleg T-shirts.
Fans traded bootleg recordings of the band's live shows.
entries.form: compound — boot + leg, from hiding bottles in a boot
entries.contrast: Also a noun (a bootleg of the concert) and a verb (to bootleg liquor). For software, movies and music, Americans more often say pirated.

entries.meaning: Informal: involving a lot of alcohol, or containing a lot of it. ---
examples: We had a long, boozy brunch on Sunday.
This eggnog is pretty boozy.
The office party was boozier than anyone expected.

entries.meaning: Very close to the line between two categories, so hard to decide; just barely acceptable or just barely a condition. ---
examples: It was a borderline call, but the umpire said he was safe.

senses.head: Accepted as the standard, classic or official version

This is the canonical example of the problem.
Fans argue about which movies are canonical in the series.

senses.head: Relating to church law or to the books accepted as part of the Bible
examples: The four canonical Gospels are Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.
Some early Christian texts were never considered canonical.

entries.meaning: Bad-tempered and always complaining or arguing. ---
examples: My cantankerous old neighbor yells at kids on his lawn.
He grew cantankerous in his old age.
The cat got more cantankerous every year.

entries.meaning: Capacious has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She pulled a notebook out of her capacious handbag.
The SUV has a capacious trunk.
The more capacious model costs $2,000 extra.
He has a capacious memory for baseball statistics.
The term is capacious enough to include almost anything.

senses.head: Having a lot of space inside
examples: She pulled a notebook out of her capacious handbag.
The SUV has a capacious trunk.
The more capacious model costs $2,000 extra.

senses.head: Wide in range; able to hold a lot of information or ideas
examples: He has a capacious memory for baseball statistics.
The term is capacious enough to include almost anything.

entries.meaning: Capital has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Write your name in capital letters.
Start every sentence with a capital letter.
Is that a capital I or a lowercase L?
Texas still uses capital punishment.
Killing a police officer is a capital crime in that state.

senses.head: Of a letter: in the large form used at the start of a sentence or a name
examples: Write your name in capital letters.
Start every sentence with a capital letter.
Is that a capital I or a lowercase L?

senses.head: Of a crime or punishment: involving the death penalty
examples: Texas still uses capital punishment.
Killing a police officer is a capital crime in that state.

entries.position: attributive only — a capital letter, a capital crime
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian капитальный (капитальный ремонт, капитальное строительство) is major, thorough or permanent in English — a major renovation, not a capital renovation. The capital (the main city) and capital (money for a business) are nouns.

entries.meaning: Based on private ownership of businesses and free markets. ---
examples: The United States has a capitalist economy.
China combines capitalist markets with one-party rule.
Is a system really capitalist if the government owns the banks?
entries.position: both — a capitalist economy, The country is capitalist
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a capitalist is a person who owns a business or invests money.

entries.meaning: Based on or too focused on private profit and free markets. ---
examples: Critics say the health care system is too capitalistic.
He grew up in a capitalistic culture that measured success in dollars.
Hong Kong was once called the most capitalistic place on earth.
entries.contrast: Capitalist is the neutral, more common word. Capitalistic often suggests 'too focused on money and profit'.

entries.meaning: Changing suddenly and without a good reason; unpredictable. ---
examples: The judge ruled that the firing was arbitrary and capricious.
Farmers here depend on capricious weather.
The new manager was even more capricious than the old one.
entries.contrast: Russian капризный about a child is usually fussy, cranky or spoiled in English. Capricious is formal and describes sudden changes with no reason — a boss, a decision, the weather.

entries.meaning: So interested or charmed that you cannot stop watching or listening. ---
examples: The children were captivated by the magician.
She watched the dancers with a captivated expression.
I've never seen an audience more captivated.
entries.position: both — a captivated audience, The audience was captivated
entries.form: -ed — the person who feels the attraction
entries.contrast: Captivated is the person watching; captivating is the thing that holds their attention: a captivating show, a captivated audience.

entries.meaning: So interesting or attractive that it holds all your attention. ---
examples: She has a captivating smile.
The documentary was absolutely captivating.
It was the most captivating performance of the night.

entries.meaning: Captive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The hostages were held captive for three weeks.
Captive elephants often live shorter lives than wild ones.
The passengers were a captive audience for the pilot's jokes.
Airport restaurants charge high prices because they have a captive market.

senses.head: Kept as a prisoner or in a cage; not free
examples: The hostages were held captive for three weeks.
Captive elephants often live shorter lives than wild ones.

senses.head: Of people: unable to leave or to choose something else
examples: The passengers were a captive audience for the pilot's jokes.
Airport restaurants charge high prices because they have a captive market.

entries.русский: пленный, в неволе; вынужденный (о слушателях, покупателях)
entries.position: both — captive animals; after a verb mostly in be held captive, take someone captive
entries.contrast: Also a noun: The captives were released.

entries.meaning: Of a drink: containing bubbles of gas. ---
examples: Do you want carbonated or still water?
Carbonated drinks can be hard on your teeth.
Is this juice carbonated?
entries.contrast: Russian газированный is not gassy: gassy means having gas in your stomach. Say carbonated water or sparkling water; soda that has lost its bubbles is flat.

entries.meaning: Able to cause cancer. ---
examples: Asbestos is highly carcinogenic.
Many chemicals in cigarette smoke are carcinogenic.
Researchers are testing which of the two compounds is more carcinogenic.
entries.form: -ic from carcinogen, a substance that causes cancer

entries.meaning: Of or relating to the heart, especially in medicine. ---
examples: He went into cardiac arrest on the tennis court.
She's a nurse in the cardiac unit.
The hospital has one of the best cardiac surgery programs in the state.
entries.position: attributive only — cardiac arrest, not The arrest was cardiac
entries.contrast: Cardiac is a medical word; everyday speech says heart: a heart attack, heart disease. Russian сердечный in the sense 'warm, kind' is warm or heartfelt, never cardiac.

entries.meaning: Cardinal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The cardinal rule in this kitchen is to wash your hands.
Lying to your customers is the cardinal sin of business.
One, two and three are cardinal numbers; first, second and third are ordinal.
North, south, east and west are the four cardinal directions.

senses.head: Most important; basic
examples: The cardinal rule in this kitchen is to wash your hands.
Lying to your customers is the cardinal sin of business.

senses.head: Of numbers and directions: basic, as in one, two, three, or north, south, east, west
examples: One, two and three are cardinal numbers; first, second and third are ordinal.
North, south, east and west are the four cardinal directions.

entries.position: attributive only — a cardinal rule, cardinal numbers
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian кардинальный (кардинальные изменения) is radical, fundamental or sweeping — sweeping changes, not cardinal changes. The noun cardinal is a Catholic church official and a red bird.

entries.meaning: Of or relating to the heart and lungs together. ---
examples: Every lifeguard must be trained in cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
After the surgery he spent six weeks in a cardiopulmonary rehab program.
A cardiopulmonary bypass machine does the work of the heart and lungs during surgery.
entries.contrast: Known mainly from cardiopulmonary resuscitation, which everyone calls CPR.

entries.meaning: Of or relating to the heart and blood vessels. ---
examples: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in the US.
Swimming is great cardiovascular exercise.
Smoking damages your cardiovascular system.
entries.contrast: In gyms the short noun is cardio: I do cardio three times a week.

entries.meaning: Happy and relaxed, without worries or responsibilities. ---
examples: We spent a carefree summer at the lake.
She seemed happy and carefree.
I was a lot more carefree before I had kids.
entries.contrast: Not careless. Carefree is a pleasant state (беззаботный); careless is a fault (небрежный, неосторожный).

entries.meaning: Kind, and showing that you care about other people. ---
examples: He's a warm, caring father.
The nurses were so caring.
She's the most caring person I know.
entries.contrast: Caring is заботливый (kind to others); careful is осторожный, аккуратный.

entries.meaning: Formal: relating to the body and sex, rather than the mind or spirit. ---
examples: The preacher warned against carnal desires.
The novel is about carnal pleasure and the guilt that follows.
In old legal language, carnal knowledge means sex.

entries.meaning: Eating meat. ---
examples: Lions and wolves are carnivorous.
The Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant.
Most sharks are carnivorous and hunt fish or seals.

entries.meaning: Covered with carpet. ---
examples: The bedrooms are carpeted, and the kitchen has tile.
We walked down a long carpeted hallway.
Is the basement carpeted?
entries.contrast: American carpet usually means wall-to-wall carpet (ковролин); a single piece on the floor is a rug.

entries.meaning: Feeling sick to your stomach from riding in a car. ---
examples: I always get carsick on mountain roads.
Let the carsick kid sit in the front seat.
She felt carsick after reading in the back seat.
entries.position: both — mostly after get or feel: I get carsick
entries.contrast: One word, like seasick and airsick. The general term is motion sickness. Russian меня укачивает is I get carsick.

entries.meaning: Cut into a shape or decorated with patterns cut into the surface. ---
examples: They sat on carved wooden chairs.
The front door is beautifully carved.
He brought me a carved stone bear from Alaska.

entries.meaning: Dealing with each situation separately instead of using one rule for all. ---
examples: Refunds are handled on a case-by-case basis.
The school takes a case-by-case approach to late homework.
The judge made case-by-case decisions about bail.
entries.position: attributive only — on a case-by-case basis
entries.form: compound — case + by + case, hyphenated before a noun
entries.contrast: After a verb it is an adverb phrase with no hyphens: We decide case by case.

entries.meaning: Cast-iron has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My grandmother cooked everything in a cast-iron skillet.
The park still has its old cast-iron benches.
You need a cast-iron stomach to eat that chili.
The suspect had a cast-iron alibi.

senses.head: Made of cast iron, a hard iron poured into a mold
examples: My grandmother cooked everything in a cast-iron skillet.
The park still has its old cast-iron benches.

senses.head: Very strong or certain; impossible to break or doubt
examples: You need a cast-iron stomach to eat that chili.
The suspect had a cast-iron alibi.

entries.position: attributive only — a cast-iron skillet; the noun is written open: made of cast iron

entries.meaning: No longer wanted by the first owner and given away or thrown out. ---
examples: The kids wore cast-off clothes from their cousins.
The shelter furnished its rooms with cast-off furniture.
He drove his father's cast-off pickup truck.
entries.form: compound — from the phrasal verb cast off
entries.contrast: The plural noun cast-offs means the things themselves: I wore my brother's cast-offs. For clothes Americans also say hand-me-down.

entries.meaning: Casual has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He tried to sound casual, but he was nervous.

The dress code at our office is casual.

Can I wear something more casual tonight?

Even a casual glance shows the numbers are wrong.

senses.head: Relaxed, and not showing much worry or interest
examples: He tried to sound casual, but he was nervous.
She has a very casual attitude toward deadlines.

senses.head: Of clothes, places or events: informal and suitable for everyday
examples: The dress code at our office is casual.
It's a casual restaurant, so jeans are fine.
Can I wear something more casual tonight?

senses.head: Not regular, close or serious
examples: We're just casual friends.
He's a casual fan who only watches the playoffs.
Even a casual glance shows the numbers are wrong.

entries.contrast: Russian случайный in the sense 'accidental' or 'random' is accidental, random or chance: a random choice, a chance meeting. Casual means relaxed, informal or not serious.

entries.meaning: Causing sudden and enormous destruction or change. ---
examples: The asteroid had a cataclysmic effect on life on earth.
Economists warned of cataclysmic consequences if the bank failed.
The flood was cataclysmic for the small town.
entries.comparison: not gradable — an extreme adjective: truly cataclysmic, not very cataclysmic

entries.meaning: Of or from Catalonia, a region of northeastern Spain, or its people or language. ---
examples: Catalan independence is a divisive issue in Spain.
We ate a traditional Catalan dish of bread rubbed with tomato.
The architect Antoni Gaudí was Catalan.
entries.position: both — Catalan food, Gaudí was Catalan
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the language and the people: She speaks Catalan. Catalonian exists but is less common. Always a capital C.

entries.meaning: Catalytic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The car needs a new catalytic converter.

The protests played a catalytic role in the reform.
The grant had a catalytic effect on the local economy.

senses.head: Speeding up a chemical reaction
examples: The car needs a new catalytic converter.
Thieves stole the catalytic converters from three cars on our street.

senses.head: Causing important changes or events to happen
examples: The protests played a catalytic role in the reform.
The grant had a catalytic effect on the local economy.

entries.meaning: Causing terrible damage or suffering; extremely bad. ---
examples: The hurricane caused catastrophic flooding.
A mistake like that could be catastrophic for the company.
It was the most catastrophic wildfire in the state's history.
entries.comparison: more/most — more catastrophic, most catastrophic; with truly or absolutely rather than very
entries.contrast: The stress moves: catastrophe is kuh-TAS-truh-fee, catastrophic is kat-uh-STRAH-fik.

entries.meaning: Catatonic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The patient remained catatonic for several days.
Doctors treated her catatonic symptoms with medication.
After finals week I sat on the couch in a catatonic state.
The kids were catatonic after six hours of video games.

senses.head: In medicine: unable to move or respond because of a mental illness
examples: The patient remained catatonic for several days.
Doctors treated her catatonic symptoms with medication.

senses.head: Informal: so shocked, tired or bored that you do not move or react
examples: After finals week I sat on the couch in a catatonic state.
The kids were catatonic after six hours of video games.

entries.meaning: Informal: easily passed from one person to another. ---
examples: Don't worry, this kind of rash isn't catching.

Is the flu catching before you have symptoms?
entries.position: predicative only — before a noun use contagious or infectious: a contagious disease
entries.form: -ing from catch, as in catch a cold

entries.meaning: Of a tune, phrase or name: pleasant and easy to remember. ---

Her refusal couldn't have been more categorical.
entries.contrast: Russian категоричный about a person is uncompromising, dogmatic or black-and-white in English. Categorical goes with statements: a categorical denial, a categorical no.

entries.meaning: Helping you release strong emotions and feel better. ---
examples: Crying at the funeral was cathartic.
Writing the book was a cathartic experience for her.
For some people, a hard workout is more cathartic than therapy.

entries.meaning: Saying unkind things about other people in a quietly nasty way. ---
examples: She made a catty remark about my dress.

The comments got cattier as the night went on.

entries.meaning: Caucasian has 2 distinct senses.

The form asks whether you are Caucasian, Black, Asian or Hispanic.
The museum has a fine collection of Caucasian rugs.
Chechen belongs to the family of Northeast Caucasian languages.

senses.head: White; of European ancestry, used as a formal racial label
examples: The suspect was described as a Caucasian male in his thirties.
The form asks whether you are Caucasian, Black, Asian or Hispanic.

senses.head: Of or from the Caucasus region between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea
examples: The museum has a fine collection of Caucasian rugs.
Chechen belongs to the family of Northeast Caucasian languages.

entries.meaning: Caught up has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I got so caught up in the book that I missed my stop.

senses.head: So involved in something that you forget other things, or cannot get free of it
examples: I got so caught up in the book that I missed my stop.
He was caught up in a bribery scandal.

senses.head: Having finished the work, reading or episodes you were behind on
examples: I'm finally caught up on my email.
Don't tell me what happens — I'm not caught up yet.

entries.position: predicative only — I got caught up in the story
entries.takes: in + noun (absorbed or involved); on + noun (no longer behind with work, reading or episodes)
entries.form: past participle of the phrasal verb catch up
entries.contrast: She caught up with us is the phrasal verb (догнала). She was caught up in the scandal and I'm caught up on my email are the adjective.

entries.meaning: Being the cause of something, or showing that one thing causes another. ---
examples: Scientists found no causal link between the vaccine and autism.

entries.contrast: Do not confuse with casual — the same letters in a different order. Causal is about cause and effect; casual is relaxed or informal.

entries.meaning: Caustic has 2 distinct senses.

She's known for her caustic wit.

senses.head: Able to burn or destroy things by chemical action
examples: Keep caustic cleaners away from children.
Lye is extremely caustic.

senses.head: Of words or humor: very critical and unkind
examples: She's known for her caustic wit.
His reviews got more caustic over the years.

entries.meaning: Giving a warning. ---

The doctor added a cautionary note about side effects.
The company's collapse serves as a cautionary example for startups.

entries.meaning: Careful to avoid danger, risk or mistakes. ---
examples: Investors are cautious about the new market.
She's a very cautious driver.
You should be more cautious with your passwords.
entries.contrast: Cautious is about avoiding risk. Careful also means doing something with attention to detail: a careful worker, careful work.

entries.meaning: Not showing enough care or concern about something important. ---

entries.contrast: False friend: Russian кавалер is a noun (a gentleman, a dance partner). The English adjective is negative: not caring enough about something serious.

entries.meaning: Of a room or space: very large, dark and often empty. ---

Their living room was even more cavernous than ours.

entries.meaning: Continuing without stopping. ---
examples: The ceaseless noise of the traffic kept me awake.
Her energy seems ceaseless.
The nurses worked with ceaseless dedication during the pandemic.

entries.meaning: Famous and praised by many people. ---
examples: She's a celebrated jazz pianist.
The chef is celebrated for his seafood.
It's one of the most celebrated novels of the century.
entries.takes: for + noun or -ing (the reason); as + noun (the role)

entries.meaning: Done or used to celebrate something. ---
examples: We had a celebratory dinner after the game.
The mood in the office was celebratory.

entries.position: both — a celebratory dinner, The mood was celebratory

senses.head: Literary: of heaven; heavenly and very beautiful
examples: The choir sang with almost celestial voices.
The ceiling painting shows celestial beings with golden wings.

entries.meaning: Of or having a disease in which the body cannot digest gluten. ---

My sister is celiac, so we cook without gluten.
The bakery has a celiac-safe menu.
entries.position: both — celiac disease; informally She's celiac
entries.contrast: American spelling celiac; British coeliac. Also a noun: a celiac, a person with the disease.

entries.meaning: Not having sex, often for religious reasons. ---
examples: Catholic priests are expected to remain celibate.
He lived a celibate life as a monk.
She decided to stay celibate for a year.

entries.meaning: Cellular has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Of or made of the cells of living things

Cellular damage builds up as we age.

senses.head: Of mobile phone networks

entries.contrast: For phones, everyday American speech shortens it to cell: a cell phone, cell service. British English says mobile.

entries.meaning: Of the Celts, ancient peoples of Europe, or of the Irish, Scottish, Welsh and Breton cultures and languages. ---

Most of the music at the festival was Celtic.
entries.contrast: Pronounced KEL-tik for the peoples, languages and music, but the Boston Celtics basketball team is SEL-tiks.

entries.meaning: With parts removed because they are considered offensive, dangerous or secret. ---
examples: TV stations showed a censored version of the movie.
Parts of the report were heavily censored.
The censored words were replaced with beeps.
entries.contrast: Not censured, which means officially criticized (осуждённый).

entries.meaning: Marking the 100th anniversary of something. ---
examples: The city is planning a big centennial celebration.
The post office issued a centennial stamp.
The university's centennial year begins in September.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: the town's centennial (столетие, сотая годовщина). British English prefers centenary.

entries.meaning: Centered has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Make sure the title is centered on the page.

Yoga helps me feel centered.
She seems more centered since she changed jobs.

senses.head: Placed in the middle of something
examples: Make sure the title is centered on the page.
The picture on that wall isn't quite centered.

senses.head: Calm, emotionally balanced and sure of what matters to you
examples: Yoga helps me feel centered.
She seems more centered since she changed jobs.

entries.contrast: American spelling; British centred. In compounds it means 'focused on': child-centered, self-centered. Centered on + noun, as in The talks were centered on trade, is the verb in the passive.

entries.meaning: Central has 3 distinct senses.
examples: We stayed at a hotel in central Chicago.
I'd rather rent something smaller in a more central neighborhood.
Family is central to her life.
Price was the central issue in the negotiations.
The house has central air and heat.
Please send the forms to the central office.

senses.head: In or near the middle of a place
examples: We stayed at a hotel in central Chicago.
I'd rather rent something smaller in a more central neighborhood.

senses.head: Most important; main
examples: Family is central to her life.
Price was the central issue in the negotiations.

senses.head: Controlled from one main place for a whole building or organization
examples: The house has central air and heat.
Please send the forms to the central office.

entries.position: both — central Chicago, Family is central to her life

entries.meaning: Of or from Central America, the land between Mexico and Colombia. ---
examples: Coffee is a major Central American export.
Many Central American families have settled in Los Angeles.
Her parents are Central American — they came from Honduras.
entries.contrast: Central America is the seven countries from Guatemala and Belize to Panama. Mexico is North American, and Latin American covers all of Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking America. No hyphen, two capitals.

entries.meaning: Controlled by one central authority or managed from one place. ---
examples: The Soviet Union had a centralized economy.

The new system is more centralized than the old one.

entries.meaning: Having political views that are neither left nor right. ---
examples: She's running as a centrist candidate.
His views on taxes are fairly centrist.
The party has become more centrist over the years.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a centrist is a politician or voter in the political center.

entries.meaning: Made of clay that has been baked hard. ---
examples: We put ceramic tile in the bathroom.
She collects ceramic bowls from Mexico.

entries.contrast: The noun ceramics means the craft or the objects: She teaches ceramics.

entries.meaning: Cerebral has 2 distinct senses.

It's a cerebral thriller with almost no action.
Her new album is more cerebral than her earlier hits.

senses.head: Of or relating to the brain

Cerebral palsy affects movement and muscle control.

senses.head: Using the mind rather than the feelings; intellectual
examples: It's a cerebral thriller with almost no action.
Her new album is more cerebral than her earlier hits.

entries.position: both — the brain sense only before a noun: a cerebral hemorrhage
entries.comparison: more/most — more cerebral, most cerebral; the brain sense is not gradable

entries.meaning: Ceremonial has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Having an official title but no real power
examples: The king's role is largely ceremonial.
In Germany the president is mostly a ceremonial figure.

entries.position: both — a ceremonial sword; after a verb mostly in the 'no real power' sense: The role is ceremonial

entries.meaning: Certifiable has 2 distinct senses.

examples: My neighbor is completely certifiable.

senses.head: Able to be officially approved or confirmed
examples: The farm has to wait three years before its crops are certifiable as organic.

entries.meaning: Certified has 2 distinct senses.

You'll need a certified copy of your birth certificate.
We bought a certified pre-owned car.

senses.head: Officially trained and approved to do a job
examples: She's a certified yoga instructor.
All our electricians are licensed and certified.
He works as a certified public accountant.

senses.head: Officially checked and guaranteed as genuine or of good quality
examples: Send the contract by certified mail.
You'll need a certified copy of your birth certificate.
We bought a certified pre-owned car.

entries.contrast: Certified mail in the US is sent with proof that it was delivered (заказное письмо с уведомлением).

entries.meaning: Cervical has 2 distinct senses.

entries.meaning: Of a birth: done by cutting through the mother's abdomen. ---

entries.contrast: In speech Americans usually say a C-section. Also a noun: She had a cesarean. British spelling caesarean.

entries.meaning: Of or from Chad, a country in north-central Africa. ---
examples: N'Djamena is the Chadian capital.
Chadian troops joined the peacekeeping mission.
Her husband is Chadian.

entries.meaning: Embarrassed and annoyed, especially because of a mistake or failure. ---
examples: He was chagrined to learn that he had missed the deadline.
She gave a chagrined smile when her phone rang during the speech.
I was less chagrined than amused by my mistake.
entries.position: both — a chagrined smile, He was chagrined
entries.contrast: Formal and literary. In conversation Americans say embarrassed or annoyed. The g is hard and the stress is on the second syllable: shuh-GRIND, rhyming with pinned.

entries.meaning: Like chalk: dry and powdery, or very pale white. ---
examples: The medicine has a chalky taste.
His face went chalky white.
This antacid is even chalkier than the other brand.

entries.meaning: Challenging has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Teaching middle school is challenging but rewarding.
The hike was more challenging than we expected.
She wanted a challenging job, not an easy one.
He gave the teacher a challenging look.
Reporters asked the mayor some challenging questions.

senses.head: Difficult in a way that tests your ability, often in an interesting way
examples: Teaching middle school is challenging but rewarding.
The hike was more challenging than we expected.
She wanted a challenging job, not an easy one.

senses.head: Of a look or question: questioning someone's authority or honesty
examples: He gave the teacher a challenging look.
Reporters asked the mayor some challenging questions.

entries.contrast: Americans often use challenging as a polite word for difficult or even bad: a challenging year, a challenging child.

entries.meaning: Happening by accident, without being planned. ---
examples: A chance meeting at a coffee shop changed her career.
The discovery of penicillin was the result of a chance observation.
His chance remark started a long argument.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb say by chance: We met by chance
entries.contrast: Chance is mostly a noun (a chance to win, by chance). Only before a noun is it an adjective meaning 'accidental': a chance meeting.

entries.meaning: Informal: risky and uncertain. ---
examples: Putting all your savings into one stock is a chancy move.
The weather in April can be chancy.
Driving over the pass got chancier after dark.

entries.meaning: Likely to change often. ---
examples: The weather in Denver is very changeable.
Teenagers' moods can be changeable.
Spring is the most changeable season here.
entries.form: -able from change, keeping the e so the g stays soft

entries.meaning: Different from before, often in an important way. ---
examples: He came back from the war a changed man.
Companies are adjusting to a changed world after the pandemic.
The neighborhood looked completely changed when I visited last year.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a changed man

entries.meaning: In the process of becoming different. ---
examples: Companies must keep up with changing technology.
We live in a fast-changing world.
Changing weather patterns are hurting farmers.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb it is the verb: Things are changing
entries.contrast: In changing room and changing table the -ing word is a noun: a room for changing clothes, a table for changing diapers.

entries.meaning: Completely confused and without order. ---
examples: The first day of school is always chaotic.
Traffic was chaotic after the power outage.
Our house got even more chaotic when the twins were born.
entries.contrast: The ch is /k/: kay-AH-tik, as in chaos (KAY-ahs).

entries.meaning: Of skin or lips: dry, rough and cracked, especially from cold or wind. ---
examples: My lips get chapped every winter.
Put some lotion on your chapped hands.
His cheeks were red and chapped from the wind.

entries.meaning: Typical of a particular person, place or thing. ---
examples: She answered with her characteristic honesty.
This kind of dark humor is characteristic of his early films.
Sharp spines are the most characteristic feature of this cactus.
entries.contrast: Russian характерный also means 'with a strong personality' (характерный актёр is a character actor). English characteristic only means 'typical'. A characteristic (noun) is a feature.

entries.meaning: Very dark gray, like the color of charcoal. ---
examples: He wore a charcoal-gray suit to the interview.
We painted the front door charcoal gray.
A charcoal-gray sky warned of snow.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (a charcoal-gray suit), usually open after a verb (The suit is charcoal gray)
entries.contrast: American spelling gray; British grey. Often shortened to charcoal: a charcoal sweater.

entries.meaning: Charged has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Immigration is a politically charged subject.
The atmosphere in the courtroom was charged.
It was the most charged debate of the campaign.
Make sure your phone is fully charged before the trip.
Electrons are negatively charged particles.

senses.head: Full of strong feelings that could lead to anger or argument
examples: Immigration is a politically charged subject.
The atmosphere in the courtroom was charged.
It was the most charged debate of the campaign.

senses.head: Holding electrical energy, or carrying an electric charge
examples: Make sure your phone is fully charged before the trip.
Electrons are negatively charged particles.

entries.contrast: He was charged with robbery is the verb charge in the passive (обвинён), not this adjective.

entries.meaning: Charismatic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's a charismatic speaker.
Voters found her warm and charismatic.
He's far more charismatic in person than on TV.
They belong to a charismatic church in Houston.
Charismatic services often include loud music and raised hands.

senses.head: Having a strong personal charm that attracts and inspires people
examples: He's a charismatic speaker.
Voters found her warm and charismatic.
He's far more charismatic in person than on TV.

senses.head: Of Christian groups: stressing gifts of the Holy Spirit, such as healing and speaking in tongues
examples: They belong to a charismatic church in Houston.
Charismatic services often include loud music and raised hands.

entries.position: both — the religious sense mostly before a noun: a charismatic church

entries.meaning: Charitable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She works for a charitable foundation.
Your donation is a charitable gift and is tax-deductible.
The most charitable explanation is that he simply forgot.
Try to be more charitable toward your coworkers.

senses.head: Relating to giving money or help to people in need
examples: She works for a charitable foundation.
Your donation is a charitable gift and is tax-deductible.

senses.head: Kind and generous in judging other people
examples: The most charitable explanation is that he simply forgot.
Try to be more charitable toward your coworkers.

entries.comparison: more/most — more charitable, most charitable; the 'charity' sense is not gradable

entries.meaning: Charmed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We were charmed by the little town.
The guests were charmed by her speech.
I was even more charmed by her sister.
She has led a charmed life.
It was a charmed season for the team.

senses.head: Pleased and delighted by someone or something
examples: We were charmed by the little town.
The guests were charmed by her speech.
I was even more charmed by her sister.

senses.head: Very lucky, as if protected by magic
examples: She has led a charmed life.
It was a charmed season for the team.

entries.position: both — the 'lucky' sense only before a noun: a charmed life
entries.takes: by or with + noun (in the 'delighted' sense)
entries.form: -ed — the person who feels the pleasure
entries.contrast: Charming is the person or thing that pleases; charmed is the person who is pleased: a charming host, charmed guests.

entries.meaning: Very pleasant and attractive. ---
examples: What a charming little house!
Her husband is smart and charming.
He was even more charming than I'd heard.
entries.contrast: Said flatly, Oh, charming is sarcastic and means 'how rude' or 'how unpleasant'.

entries.meaning: Of a plane, bus or boat: hired by a group for a particular trip. ---
examples: The team flew to Denver on a chartered plane.
We took a chartered bus to the game.
They went deep-sea fishing on a chartered boat.
entries.contrast: A charter flight (noun + noun) is at least as common as a chartered flight. Chartered accountant is British; Americans say certified public accountant or CPA.

entries.meaning: Not having sex, or not involving sexual feeling. ---
examples: Their romance was chaste and old-fashioned.
He gave her a chaste kiss on the cheek.
The nuns took a vow to remain chaste.

entries.meaning: Chatty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Our Uber driver was very chatty.
She gets chattier after a glass of wine.
She sent me a long, chatty email.
The book is written in a chatty style.

senses.head: Of a person: liking to talk in a friendly way
examples: Our Uber driver was very chatty.
She gets chattier after a glass of wine.

senses.head: Of writing or speech: informal and friendly
examples: She sent me a long, chatty email.
The book is written in a chatty style.

entries.meaning: Chauvinistic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His chauvinistic comments about female engineers got him fired.
Some ads from the 1960s look shockingly chauvinistic today.
The most chauvinistic jokes came from the manager himself.
The speech was full of chauvinistic national pride.
Chauvinistic nationalism grew in the years before the war.

senses.head: Believing that men are better than women, and treating women unfairly
examples: His chauvinistic comments about female engineers got him fired.
Some ads from the 1960s look shockingly chauvinistic today.
The most chauvinistic jokes came from the manager himself.

senses.head: Believing that your own country or group is better than all others
examples: The speech was full of chauvinistic national pride.
Chauvinistic nationalism grew in the years before the war.

entries.contrast: In American English chauvinist most often means male chauvinist, a man who treats women as inferior. Russian шовинизм is usually about nationality; English uses chauvinistic that way too, but less often.

entries.meaning: Cheap has 4 distinct senses.
examples: Gas is cheaper in New Jersey than in New York.
We found a cheap flight to Miami.
This is the cheapest phone they sell.
The chair broke because it was made of cheap plastic.
Her shoes looked cheap.
Don't be so cheap — leave a real tip.
My uncle is too cheap to turn on the heat.
Bringing up his divorce was a cheap shot.
Jokes about her weight were a cheap way to get laughs.

senses.head: Low in price
examples: Gas is cheaper in New Jersey than in New York.
We found a cheap flight to Miami.
This is the cheapest phone they sell.

senses.head: Of poor quality
examples: The chair broke because it was made of cheap plastic.
Her shoes looked cheap.

senses.head: Of a person: not willing to spend money
examples: Don't be so cheap — leave a real tip.
My uncle is too cheap to turn on the heat.

senses.head: Unfair or unkind in a way that shows no respect
examples: Bringing up his divorce was a cheap shot.
Jokes about her weight were a cheap way to get laughs.

entries.contrast: Cheap often suggests poor quality, so to praise a low price say inexpensive or affordable. About a person, American cheap means 'stingy' (жадный), not дешёвый. Cheaply is the adverb, though buy it cheap is common in speech.

entries.meaning: Cheating has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She finally left her cheating husband.
The song is about a lying, cheating boyfriend.
Fans booed the cheating team.
The cheating students were suspended for a week.

senses.head: Having a secret sexual relationship with someone other than your partner
examples: She finally left her cheating husband.
The song is about a lying, cheating boyfriend.

senses.head: Breaking the rules to win or get an advantage
examples: Fans booed the cheating team.
The cheating students were suspended for a week.

entries.position: attributive only — after a verb it is the verb: He is cheating
entries.contrast: In a cheating scandal the -ing word is a noun (the act of cheating), not this adjective.

entries.meaning: Of or from Chechnya, a republic in the North Caucasus, or its people or language. ---
examples: Grozny is the Chechen capital.
Many Chechen refugees settled in Austria and Germany.
Her grandparents were Chechen.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the people and the language: He speaks Chechen.

entries.meaning: Checked has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She wore a red-and-white checked shirt.
The tablecloth in the kitchen is checked.
Each checked bag costs thirty-five dollars.
Put the shampoo in your checked luggage.

senses.head: Of cloth: having a pattern of squares in different colors
examples: She wore a red-and-white checked shirt.
The tablecloth in the kitchen is checked.

senses.head: Of luggage: handed to an airline to carry in the hold of the plane
examples: Each checked bag costs thirty-five dollars.
Put the shampoo in your checked luggage.

entries.position: both — the luggage sense only before a noun: a checked bag
entries.form: -ed from check (a square pattern; to hand over luggage)
entries.contrast: For patterns Americans more often say checkered or plaid. The opposite of checked luggage is carry-on luggage.

entries.meaning: Checkered has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The race ends when the checkered flag waves.
The diner has a black-and-white checkered floor.
The mayor has a checkered past.
The company has a checkered history with safety regulators.

senses.head: Having a pattern of squares in two colors, like a checkerboard
examples: The race ends when the checkered flag waves.
The diner has a black-and-white checkered floor.

senses.head: Having good and bad parts, especially trouble or scandal
examples: The mayor has a checkered past.
The company has a checkered history with safety regulators.

entries.position: both — the 'mixed history' sense only before a noun: a checkered past
entries.form: -ed from checker, a square on a checkerboard
entries.contrast: American spelling; British chequered. A checkered past is not a colorful past but one with scandals or failures in it.

entries.meaning: Slightly rude or disrespectful, often in a funny or charming way. ---
examples: He gave me a cheeky grin.
Don't be cheeky with your grandmother.
The cheekiest kid in class asked the principal how old she was.
entries.contrast: More common in British English. Americans use it for playful, slightly rude behavior; sassy is the more American word.

entries.meaning: Cheerful has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She's always cheerful in the morning.
The nurse greeted us with a cheerful smile.
You seem more cheerful today.
They painted the kitchen a cheerful yellow.
The waiting room was small but cheerful.

senses.head: Happy and positive in the way you look or behave
examples: She's always cheerful in the morning.
The nurse greeted us with a cheerful smile.
You seem more cheerful today.

senses.head: Of a place or color: bright and pleasant
examples: They painted the kitchen a cheerful yellow.
The waiting room was small but cheerful.

entries.meaning: Happy and friendly, often in an obvious way. ---
examples: The waiter gave us a cheery hello.
The room felt cheerier with the new curtains.
She's annoyingly cheery at six in the morning.

entries.meaning: Cheesy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kids love cheesy pasta.
This pizza is cheesier than the one we had last week.
He told a cheesy joke about accountants.
The movie is really cheesy, but I love it.
That was the cheesiest pickup line I've ever heard.

senses.head: Tasting of cheese or containing a lot of cheese
examples: The kids love cheesy pasta.
This pizza is cheesier than the one we had last week.

senses.head: Informal: cheap, silly or too sentimental in an embarrassing way
examples: He told a cheesy joke about accountants.
The movie is really cheesy, but I love it.
That was the cheesiest pickup line I've ever heard.

entries.contrast: A cheesy grin is a wide, forced smile, like the one people make when they say 'cheese' for a photo.

entries.meaning: Of or produced by chemistry or chemicals. ---
examples: Rust forms through a chemical reaction between iron and oxygen.
The factory was fined for a chemical spill.
The difference between the two samples is chemical, not physical.
entries.position: both — a chemical reaction, The change is chemical, not physical
entries.contrast: Russian химический before a subject or a person is often the noun chemistry in English: a chemistry teacher, a chemistry lab, not a chemical teacher. Chemicals (noun) are substances.

entries.meaning: Loved, valued and kept with great care. ---
examples: The ring is one of her most cherished possessions.
I have cherished memories of summers at the lake.
Free speech is a cherished American value.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a cherished memory

entries.meaning: Bright red, like a ripe cherry. ---
examples: He drove a cherry-red convertible.
Her lipstick was cherry red.
The cherry-red barn stood out against the snow.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (a cherry-red car), usually open after a verb (The car is cherry red)
entries.contrast: Russian вишнёвый is a dark red, closer to burgundy or dark red; cherry-red is a bright, shiny red.

entries.meaning: Looking sweet and innocent, often with a round face, like a small child or angel. ---
examples: The baby had a cherubic face and big blue eyes.
With his round red cheeks, he looked cherubic in his choir robe.
He looks cherubic, but he's the class troublemaker.

entries.meaning: Reddish brown, like the color of a chestnut. ---
examples: She has long chestnut hair.
He rode a chestnut mare in the parade.
Her hair was chestnut when she was young.
entries.position: both — chestnut hair, Her hair is chestnut
entries.contrast: Chestnut is mainly a noun (the nut or the tree). As a color it is used mostly for hair and horses; for Russian каштановые волосы Americans also say brown or auburn hair.

entries.meaning: Made to be chewed before swallowing, not swallowed whole. ---
examples: The kids take chewable vitamins every morning.
Are these allergy tablets chewable, or do I swallow them?
The pharmacist gave me a chewable form of the medicine.

entries.meaning: Needing a lot of chewing; soft but firm or sticky. ---
examples: I like my chocolate chip cookies soft and chewy.
The steak was dry and chewy.
This bagel is chewier than the ones from the other bakery.

entries.meaning: Fashionable and elegant in style. ---
examples: She always looks chic, even in jeans.
They opened a chic little wine bar downtown.
The new lobby is much more chic than the old one.
entries.contrast: Pronounced SHEEK, not like chick. Chic means elegant in a fashionable, understated way; Russian шикарный can also mean luxurious and showy, which is closer to lavish or flashy.

entries.meaning: Afraid to do something; cowardly. ---
examples: Come on, jump in — don't be chicken!
I was too chicken to ask her out.
Everyone knew he was chicken when it came to roller coasters.
entries.position: predicative only — never before a noun
entries.comparison: more/most — more chicken; usually too chicken or so chicken
entries.contrast: In chicken soup or chicken wings, chicken is a noun used as a modifier, not this adjective. The verb phrase chicken out means to lose your nerve (He chickened out at the last minute), and the noun works too: You're such a chicken!

entries.meaning: Built around children's needs and interests rather than adults' plans. ---
examples: The school takes a child-centered approach to learning.
Our pediatrician's office is very child-centered.
Parenting has become far more child-centered than it was fifty years ago.

entries.meaning: Having no children. ---
examples: They were a childless couple in their forties.
She stayed childless by choice.
The survey compared parents with childless adults.

entries.meaning: Of or from Chile, its people or its culture. ---
examples: We had a bottle of Chilean wine with dinner.
Her husband is Chilean.
The Chilean coastline stretches for thousands of miles.
entries.contrast: Always a capital C, unlike Russian чилийский. It is also a noun: a Chilean. Some Americans say chi-LAY-uhn, closer to Spanish.

entries.meaning: Chilling has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The movie tells a chilling story about a small-town murder.
His calm description of the crime was chilling.
The most chilling part was the silence afterward.
Critics say the new law will have a chilling effect on free speech.
The lawsuits had a chilling effect on reporters.

senses.head: Frightening, especially in a cold, quiet way
examples: The movie tells a chilling story about a small-town murder.
His calm description of the crime was chilling.
The most chilling part was the silence afterward.

senses.head: Making people afraid to act or speak freely; used mainly in a chilling effect
examples: Critics say the new law will have a chilling effect on free speech.
The lawsuits had a chilling effect on reporters.

entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling; from chill
entries.contrast: Chilling frightens you; chilled means made cold (chilled wine). In slang, We're just chilling is the verb chill, meaning relaxing, not this adjective.

entries.meaning: Chintzy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The hotel room had chintzy plastic furniture.
That trophy looks kind of chintzy.
They put up the chintziest decorations I've ever seen.
Don't be chintzy — leave a decent tip.
The company has always been chintzy about raises.

senses.head: Cheap-looking and poorly made
examples: The hotel room had chintzy plastic furniture.
That trophy looks kind of chintzy.
They put up the chintziest decorations I've ever seen.

senses.head: Unwilling to spend money; stingy
examples: Don't be chintzy — leave a decent tip.
The company has always been chintzy about raises.

entries.form: -y from chintz, a cheap printed cotton

entries.meaning: Cheerful and full of energy. ---
examples: You're awfully chipper for seven in the morning.
She sounded chipper on the phone.
He seemed a lot more chipper after his nap.

entries.meaning: Cheerful and lively, sometimes a little too bright. ---
examples: The receptionist was annoyingly chirpy.
She left a chirpy message on my voicemail.
He's always chirpier after his first cup of coffee.
entries.form: -y from chirp, a bird's short high sound

entries.meaning: Having strong, sharp, clearly defined lines, especially of a face or muscles. ---
examples: The actor is known for his chiseled jaw.
His arms looked chiseled after months at the gym.
She has high, chiseled cheekbones.
entries.form: -ed from chisel, a tool for cutting stone or wood
entries.contrast: American spelling has one l: chiseled. Chiselled is British.

entries.meaning: Polite, kind and protective, especially of a man toward women. ---
examples: It was chivalrous of him to give up his seat.
He made a chivalrous offer to walk her home.
Some women find the gesture chivalrous; others find it old-fashioned.
entries.contrast: It starts with a sh sound, not ch.

entries.meaning: Completely full; packed. ---
examples: The fridge is chock-full of leftovers.
Her essay was chock-full of typos.
It's a guidebook chock-full of useful tips.
entries.position: predicative only — or right after a noun: a book chock-full of ideas

entries.meaning: Choice has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The butcher saves the choicest cuts for his regular customers.
We got choice seats near the stage.
The lake has some choice spots for fishing.
He had a few choice words for the referee.
When she saw the bill, she used some choice language.

senses.head: Of very high quality; carefully picked as the best
examples: The butcher saves the choicest cuts for his regular customers.
We got choice seats near the stage.
The lake has some choice spots for fishing.

senses.head: Angry or rude; used mainly in a few choice words
examples: He had a few choice words for the referee.
When she saw the bill, she used some choice language.

entries.contrast: Usually a noun (make a choice). The adjective goes only before a noun and sounds a little formal, except in a few choice words, which means angry or rude words, not carefully chosen polite ones.

entries.meaning: Very careful about what you choose; hard to please. ---
examples: She's choosy about the guys she dates.
He's a choosy eater, so we never go anywhere new.
Cats are often choosier about food than dogs.

entries.meaning: Cut into small pieces with a knife. ---
examples: Add a cup of chopped onions.
Top the salad with chopped walnuts.
Make sure the garlic is finely chopped.

entries.meaning: Choppy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The lake was too choppy for kayaking.
We hit choppy water on the way back.
The bay gets choppier in the afternoon.
The video call was choppy, so I couldn't hear her.
His writing is choppy, with lots of short sentences.

senses.head: Of water: rough, with many small waves
examples: The lake was too choppy for kayaking.
We hit choppy water on the way back.
The bay gets choppier in the afternoon.

senses.head: Not smooth; broken into short, jerky parts
examples: The video call was choppy, so I couldn't hear her.
His writing is choppy, with lots of short sentences.

entries.meaning: For or sung by a choir. ---
examples: She directs the choral program at the high school.
They performed a choral version of the hymn.
The concert features choral music from the 1700s.
entries.contrast: The ch is a k sound, and in American English choral sounds the same as coral.

entries.meaning: Chronic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She has suffered from chronic back pain for years.
Diabetes is a chronic disease.
His cough eventually became chronic.
The city has a chronic shortage of affordable housing.
He's a chronic liar.
Chronic lateness got her fired.

senses.head: Of an illness or pain: lasting a long time or keeping coming back
examples: She has suffered from chronic back pain for years.
Diabetes is a chronic disease.
His cough eventually became chronic.

senses.head: Of a problem or habit: always happening; habitual
examples: The city has a chronic shortage of affordable housing.
He's a chronic liar.
Chronic lateness got her fired.

entries.contrast: British informal chronic meaning 'very bad' (The food was chronic) is not used in American English.

entries.meaning: Arranged in the order in which events happened. ---
examples: List your jobs in reverse chronological order.
The museum tells the city's story in chronological order.
The novel's timeline isn't strictly chronological.

entries.meaning: Slightly fat, in a round and often cute way. ---
examples: Look at the baby's chubby little cheeks!
I was a chubby kid, but I grew out of it.
Our cat has gotten chubbier since we moved.
entries.contrast: Friendly when said about babies and cheeks; about an adult it can sound rude. The neutral words are heavy and overweight.

entries.meaning: Very friendly, sometimes too friendly. ---
examples: He's gotten pretty chummy with the boss.
The two senators seemed awfully chummy at dinner.
They're chummier now than they were in college.
entries.form: -y from chum, an old word for a friend

entries.meaning: Chunky has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She wore a chunky knit sweater.
Chunky gold necklaces are back in style.
These boots have a chunkier heel.
Do you like smooth or chunky peanut butter?
The salsa is nice and chunky.
He was a chunky linebacker from Ohio.
Our dog is a chunky little beagle.

senses.head: Thick, heavy and solid-looking
examples: She wore a chunky knit sweater.
Chunky gold necklaces are back in style.
These boots have a chunkier heel.

senses.head: Of food: containing pieces rather than smooth
examples: Do you like smooth or chunky peanut butter?
The salsa is nice and chunky.

senses.head: Of a person or animal: short, broad and a little heavy
examples: He was a chunky linebacker from Ohio.
Our dog is a chunky little beagle.

entries.meaning: Going to church regularly. ---
examples: She grew up in a churchgoing family in Georgia.
The town is small and mostly churchgoing.
Churchgoing Americans are less common than they were in the 1970s.

entries.meaning: Rude and unfriendly, especially when you ought to be grateful or polite. ---
examples: It would be churlish to complain about a free meal.
He gave a churlish reply and walked away.
Refusing their invitation seemed churlish.
entries.takes: to-infinitive, mainly in It would be churlish to...
entries.form: -ish from churl, an old word for a rude man

entries.meaning: Cinematic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Hitchcock's cinematic techniques are still studied today.
It was her first cinematic role.
The video game has cinematic graphics.
The new season feels even more cinematic than the last.
Her novels are so cinematic that they read like screenplays.

senses.head: Relating to movies and moviemaking
examples: Hitchcock's cinematic techniques are still studied today.
It was her first cinematic role.

senses.head: Looking or feeling like a movie; dramatic and visual
examples: The video game has cinematic graphics.
The new season feels even more cinematic than the last.
Her novels are so cinematic that they read like screenplays.

entries.comparison: more/most — more cinematic in the 'like a movie' sense; the first sense is not gradable

entries.meaning: Relating to the body's natural 24-hour cycle. ---
examples: Jet lag throws off your circadian rhythm.
Blue light at night can disrupt circadian cycles.
Scientists study the circadian clock in fruit flies.

entries.meaning: Long and indirect; not going straight to a place or to the point. ---
examples: We took a circuitous route to avoid traffic.
His explanation was long and circuitous.
The trail to the summit is more circuitous than it looks on the map.

entries.meaning: Relating to the movement of blood through the body. ---
examples: The heart is the center of the circulatory system.
Smoking can cause circulatory problems.
He has a rare circulatory disorder.

entries.meaning: Careful not to take risks or say too much. ---
examples: The senator was circumspect about her plans.
Investors have become more circumspect since the crash.
He gave a circumspect answer.

entries.meaning: Based on facts that suggest something is true but do not prove it directly. ---
examples: The case against him was purely circumstantial.
Prosecutors relied on circumstantial evidence.
The jury convicted her on circumstantial evidence alone.

entries.meaning: Covering or happening in the whole city. ---
examples: The mayor announced a citywide curfew.
There was a citywide power outage last night.
The recycling program is now citywide.
entries.contrast: Also an adverb: The ban applies citywide.

entries.meaning: Civic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Voting is a civic duty.
She's active in several civic organizations.
The school teaches civic responsibility.
The concert is at the civic center.
The new park is a source of civic pride.

senses.head: Relating to the duties and activities of citizens
examples: Voting is a civic duty.
She's active in several civic organizations.
The school teaches civic responsibility.

senses.head: Relating to a town or city and its public life
examples: The concert is at the civic center.
The new park is a source of civic pride.

entries.contrast: Civic is about a citizen's part in the life of a town or country (civic duty, civic pride). Civil is about citizens as opposed to the military or the church, and also means polite (civil rights, a civil answer). Civilian means not in the armed forces (civilian clothes).

entries.meaning: Civil has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Martin Luther King Jr. was a leader of the civil rights movement.
The country was torn apart by civil war.
They had a civil ceremony at city hall instead of a church wedding.
She filed a civil lawsuit against the company.
It's a civil case, so nobody is going to prison.
Try to stay civil even if he gets angry.
They're divorced, but they're civil to each other.
The debate was more civil than anyone expected.

senses.head: Relating to ordinary citizens and their rights, not to the military or religion
examples: Martin Luther King Jr. was a leader of the civil rights movement.
The country was torn apart by civil war.
They had a civil ceremony at city hall instead of a church wedding.

senses.head: In law: about private disputes between people or companies, not about crimes
examples: She filed a civil lawsuit against the company.
It's a civil case, so nobody is going to prison.

senses.head: Polite, but not especially friendly
examples: Try to stay civil even if he gets angry.
They're divorced, but they're civil to each other.
The debate was more civil than anyone expected.

entries.position: both — but civil meaning 'of citizens' or 'in law' goes only before a noun
entries.comparison: more/most — more civil, most civil in the 'polite' sense; the other senses are not gradable
entries.opposite: uncivil, rude (polite sense); military (citizens sense); criminal (law sense)
entries.contrast: Civil and civic both translate as гражданский: civil rights, civil war and a civil ceremony are about citizens as opposed to the army or the church, while civic duty is about taking part in public life. Civilian clothes (not civil clothes) are clothes that are not a uniform.

entries.meaning: Not belonging to the armed forces or the police. ---
examples: He found it hard to adjust to civilian life after the Army.
The bombing caused heavy civilian casualties.
The officers were in civilian clothes.
entries.contrast: Usually a noun (Two civilians were hurt). The adjective goes before a noun: civilian clothes, civilian life; not civil clothes.

entries.meaning: Civilized has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Torture has no place in a civilized society.
Every civilized nation has laws against slavery.
Let's discuss this like civilized adults.
Dinner at eight is a much more civilized hour than dinner at five.
The divorce was surprisingly civilized.

senses.head: Of a society: having an advanced system of laws, government and culture
examples: Torture has no place in a civilized society.
Every civilized nation has laws against slavery.

senses.head: Polite, calm and reasonable; also pleasant and comfortable
examples: Let's discuss this like civilized adults.
Dinner at eight is a much more civilized hour than dinner at five.
The divorce was surprisingly civilized.

entries.contrast: American spelling uses z: civilized, not civilised.

entries.meaning: Dressed in something, or covered with something. ---

Two men clad in black stood by the door.
The building is clad in glass and steel.
entries.position: predicative only — or right after a noun: a woman clad in black; before a noun only in compounds like ivy-clad

entries.meaning: Able to see the future or know things beyond the normal senses. ---
examples: She claims to have clairvoyant powers.
I'm not clairvoyant — you have to tell me what's wrong.
He said a clairvoyant dream warned him about the crash.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a clairvoyant. Often used as a joke about someone who guesses well.

entries.meaning: Unpleasantly damp and sticky, and usually cold. ---
examples: My hands get clammy when I'm nervous.
The basement air was cold and clammy.
His forehead felt clammier by the minute.
entries.русский: липкий и влажный, холодный и потный

entries.meaning: Done secretly, often because it is illegal or not allowed. ---

entries.meaning: Clarifying has 2 distinct senses.

This clarifying toner works well on oily skin.

senses.head: Making something easier to understand
examples: Can I ask a clarifying question?
The lawyer issued a clarifying statement.
Talking it through with my sister was really clarifying.

senses.head: Of a beauty product: removing oil and buildup
examples: Use a clarifying shampoo once a week.
This clarifying toner works well on oily skin.

entries.position: both — but the cosmetics sense only before a noun
entries.comparison: more/most — more clarifying in the first sense

entries.meaning: Very aware of social class and of differences between classes. ---

My grandmother was very class-conscious.
Americans are more class-conscious than they like to admit.

entries.meaning: Classified has 2 distinct senses.

The full report remains classified.

senses.head: Officially secret and available only to certain people
examples: He was charged with leaking classified documents.
I'm sorry, that information is classified.
The full report remains classified.

senses.head: Of ads: short, private and arranged by subject in a newspaper or on a website
examples: She found her first apartment in the classified ads.
He sold his old truck through the classified section.

entries.position: both — but classified ads only before a noun

entries.meaning: Classless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Marx imagined a classless society.
America likes to see itself as classless, but it isn't.
Mocking the injured player was a classless move.

senses.head: Without divisions between social classes

senses.head: Informal: rude and lacking good manners, especially in sports

examples: It was classy of him to congratulate the winner.

senses.head: Of a place or situation: making you feel shut in
examples: The apartment was dark and claustrophobic.
Living with my parents again felt claustrophobic.
The basement office is even more claustrophobic than the old one.

entries.meaning: Neat, tidy and respectable-looking, often with short hair. ---

entries.meaning: Cleansing has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Making you feel emotionally fresh and free of bad feelings
examples: Take a deep, cleansing breath.
Crying can be very cleansing.
Finally telling the truth felt cleansing.

entries.meaning: Seeing a situation clearly and realistically, without illusions. ---

examples: The drug is still in clinical trials.

His writing is a little too clinical for my taste.

senses.head: Of a room or building: plain, very clean and unwelcoming, like a hospital
examples: The new office feels cold and clinical.
They painted over the clinical white walls with a warm yellow.

entries.position: both — but the medical sense mostly before a noun

entries.contrast: About a person, a style or a room, clinical is usually criticism: cold and without feeling. It is not an intensifier like Russian клинический in клинический идиот.

entries.meaning: Attached with a clip rather than pinned, tied or put through a hole. ---

examples: The house has a neatly clipped hedge.

entries.meaning: Blocked so that liquid, air or traffic cannot move through easily. ---

Her collected essays came out last fall.
