senses.head: Having traveled and seen a lot of the world; sophisticated
examples: Her cosmopolitan friends seemed to have lived everywhere.
He's much more cosmopolitan than his small-town parents.

entries.contrast: In English cosmopolitan is a compliment, with none of the negative Soviet sense of космополит. A Cosmopolitan is also a cocktail.

entries.meaning: Giving good results for the money spent. ---
examples: Solar panels are a cost-effective way to cut your bills.
Buying in bulk is usually more cost-effective.
We need the most cost-effective solution, not the fanciest.

entries.meaning: Doing a job well without wasting money. ---
examples: The new engines are more cost-efficient than the old ones.
We're looking for a cost-efficient way to ship packages.
Is it really cost-efficient to repair this old printer?

entries.meaning: From or relating to Costa Rica. ---
examples: We drank strong Costa Rican coffee every morning.
Her husband is Costa Rican.
The Costa Rican rainforest is full of birds.
entries.contrast: A Costa Rican is also a person from Costa Rica. Both words take capital letters.

entries.meaning: In grammar, of a noun: having a plural form and used with a or an. ---
examples: Chair is a countable noun, but furniture is not.
Use many with countable nouns and much with uncountable ones.
In English, advice is not countable.
entries.contrast: Many nouns that are countable in Russian are uncountable in English: advice, news, information, furniture, luggage. Say a piece of advice, never an advice.

entries.meaning: Moving in the direction opposite to the hands of a clock. ---
examples: Give the lid a counterclockwise turn to open it.
The runners move in a counterclockwise direction around the track.
Hurricanes north of the equator have a counterclockwise spin.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a counterclockwise turn
entries.contrast: British English says anticlockwise. The word is most often an adverb: turn the knob counterclockwise.

entries.meaning: Made to look exactly like the real thing in order to trick people. ---
examples: Police found thousands of dollars in counterfeit bills.
The market is full of counterfeit designer bags.
The bank said the check was counterfeit.
entries.contrast: Counterfeit is used mostly for money and branded goods; for a signature or document forged is more usual. Counterfeit is also a noun and a verb.

entries.meaning: Different from what you would expect or naturally think is true. ---
examples: It seems counterintuitive, but hot tea can cool you down.
The results of the study were counterintuitive.
Oddly, the most counterintuitive part of the plan worked best.

entries.meaning: Having the opposite effect to the one you want. ---
examples: Yelling at kids is often counterproductive.
Cutting the budget again would be counterproductive.
Nothing is more counterproductive than a meeting about having too many meetings.

entries.meaning: Opposed to a revolution and trying to reverse it. ---
examples: The rebels were accused of counterrevolutionary activity.
The army put down a counterrevolutionary uprising.
The new regime called every critic counterrevolutionary.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a counterrevolutionary is a person who fights a revolution.

entries.meaning: Meant to prevent or fight terrorism. ---
examples: A counterterrorist unit was sent to the airport.
The FBI runs counterterrorist training for local police.
The two countries agreed to share counterterrorist intelligence.
entries.contrast: Americans often use the noun counterterrorism before another noun instead: counterterrorism officials. A counterterrorist is also a person.

entries.meaning: Too many to count; very many. ---
examples: I've told you countless times to lock the door.
The storm destroyed countless homes.
She spent countless hours practicing the piano.
entries.contrast: Only before a plural noun. After a verb say too many to count: the mistakes were too many to count.

entries.meaning: Made, cooked or decorated in a simple, traditional rural way. ---
examples: We had country-style ribs and cornbread.
The kitchen has a big country-style wooden table.
Breakfast is country-style, with biscuits and gravy.
entries.contrast: Country here means the countryside, not a nation. Country-style ribs are a meaty cut of pork, not a recipe.

entries.meaning: Happening or existing in every part of a country. ---
examples: Police launched a countrywide search for the missing girl.
Within a week the strike was countrywide.
There is a countrywide shortage of nurses.
entries.contrast: Also an adverb: the show airs countrywide. Americans more often say nationwide.

entries.meaning: Brave; willing to do something dangerous or difficult. ---
examples: It was a courageous decision to speak out.
The firefighters were incredibly courageous.
She's the most courageous person I know.
entries.contrast: The stress moves: KUR-ij, but kuh-RAY-juhs.

entries.meaning: Required by the decision of a court of law. ---
examples: He had to attend court-ordered anger management classes.
The court-ordered sale of the house happened in May.
The company made court-ordered payments to its workers.
entries.contrast: After a verb use the passive, with no hyphen: the test was ordered by the court.

entries.meaning: Polite and respectful to other people. ---
examples: The hotel staff were friendly and courteous.
Please be courteous to other passengers.
The officer was more courteous than I expected.

entries.meaning: Polite, graceful and formal in an old-fashioned way. ---
examples: He greeted her with a courtly bow.
My grandfather had courtly Southern manners.
He was the most courtly man in the office, always holding doors.
entries.contrast: An -ly adjective, not an adverb: say in a courtly way.

entries.meaning: Secret or hidden, especially done by spies or government agents. ---
examples: The CIA ran a covert operation in the region.
She gave him a covert glance across the table.
After the arrests, the group became more covert.

entries.meaning: Wanted very much by many people. ---
examples: She won the coveted first prize.
Tickets to the final are the most coveted in sports.
Jobs at the company are highly coveted.

entries.meaning: Wanting very much to have what belongs to someone else (formal). ---
examples: He cast a covetous eye on his neighbor's new truck.
She was covetous of her sister's success.
Wealth only made him more covetous.

entries.meaning: Coy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She gave him a coy smile.
Don't be coy. You know you like him.
The actress is coy about her age.
The company has been more coy about its plans than usual.

senses.head: Pretending to be shy, often in a playful way to attract someone
examples: She gave him a coy smile.
Don't be coy. You know you like him.

senses.head: Unwilling to give information about something
examples: The actress is coy about her age.
The company has been more coy about its plans than usual.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — coyer, coyest; more coy, most coy

entries.meaning: Cozy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We found a cozy little cafe near the river.
The cabin was warm and cozy.
This is the coziest chair in the house.
Critics attacked the senator's cozy relationship with oil companies.
The regulators got a little too cozy with the banks.

senses.head: Warm, comfortable and pleasant, often because it is small
examples: We found a cozy little cafe near the river.
The cabin was warm and cozy.
This is the coziest chair in the house.

senses.head: Too close or friendly, in a way that seems unfair or dishonest (disapproving)
examples: Critics attacked the senator's cozy relationship with oil companies.
The regulators got a little too cozy with the banks.

entries.contrast: British spelling is cosy; American is cozy.

entries.meaning: In a bad mood and easily annoyed (informal). ---
examples: I get crabby when I'm hungry.
A crabby old man yelled at us to get off his lawn.
The kids are always crabbier after a long car ride.

entries.meaning: Very skillful; expert (informal). ---
examples: He's a crack shot with a rifle.
A crack team of lawyers handled the case.
Crack troops were sent to guard the border.
entries.contrast: Only before a noun, and mostly in a crack shot, a crack team, crack troops. Crack is far more often a noun (a thin break; the drug) or a verb.

entries.meaning: Cracked has 3 distinct senses.
examples: I need to replace my cracked phone screen.
Her lips were dry and cracked from the cold.
Don't drink from that cracked glass.
He answered in a cracked voice.
Her voice sounded cracked and tired.
Season the steak with salt and cracked black pepper.
The bread is made with cracked wheat.

senses.head: Having thin lines of breakage on the surface
examples: I need to replace my cracked phone screen.
Her lips were dry and cracked from the cold.
Don't drink from that cracked glass.

senses.head: Of a voice: rough and uneven, as if about to break
examples: He answered in a cracked voice.
Her voice sounded cracked and tired.

senses.head: Of pepper, grain or nuts: broken into rough pieces
examples: Season the steak with salt and cracked black pepper.
The bread is made with cracked wheat.

entries.position: both — sense 3 only before a noun
entries.contrast: Not all it's cracked up to be (not as good as people say) comes from the phrasal verb crack up, not from this adjective.

entries.meaning: Crafty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The crafty old fox got into the henhouse again.
He's craftier than he looks, so watch him.
I'm not very crafty, so I bought the decorations.
My daughter loves crafty projects like making cards.

senses.head: Clever at getting what you want, often by tricking people
examples: The crafty old fox got into the henhouse again.
He's craftier than he looks, so watch him.

senses.head: Good at making things by hand, or involving handmade crafts (informal)
examples: I'm not very crafty, so I bought the decorations.
My daughter loves crafty projects like making cards.

entries.meaning: Craggy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They hiked along the craggy coastline.
The craggiest peaks were covered in snow.
The actor has a craggy, handsome face.
His face had grown craggy with age.

senses.head: Steep and rough, with a lot of large rocks
examples: They hiked along the craggy coastline.
The craggiest peaks were covered in snow.

senses.head: Of a man's face: with deep lines, in a strong and attractive way
examples: The actor has a craggy, handsome face.
His face had grown craggy with age.

entries.meaning: Too small for the people or things in it, so there is not enough room. ---
examples: Four of us shared a cramped two-room apartment.
The back seat is a little cramped for three adults.
Airline seats seem more cramped every year.

entries.meaning: Bad-tempered and easily annoyed, often because you are tired or hungry. ---
examples: The baby gets cranky when she misses her nap.
My cranky neighbor complains about everything.
Dad is always crankier before his morning coffee.
entries.contrast: This is the American meaning. In British English cranky more often means strange or eccentric.

entries.meaning: Very bad or of poor quality (rude slang). ---
examples: I had a really crappy day at work.
The hotel room was small and crappy.
This is the crappiest phone I've ever owned.
entries.contrast: Rude but common in casual American speech; avoid it at work and in writing. Softer choices: lousy, crummy, bad.

entries.meaning: Rude and showing no sensitivity or good taste, often about money. ---
examples: It was crass to ask how much she paid for the house.
The ad was a crass attempt to sell toys to toddlers.
Of all his jokes that night, that one was the most crass.

entries.meaning: Cowardly; lacking courage (formal, disapproving). ---
examples: The senator's craven silence angered his voters.
Giving in to the threats was a craven surrender.
I can't think of a more craven act than blaming your own staff.

entries.meaning: Wild and out of control, like someone who has gone mad. ---
examples: Crazed fans pushed toward the stage.
He had a crazed look in his eyes.
She was crazed with grief after the accident.
entries.contrast: Often in compounds: power-crazed, drug-crazed, money-crazed.

entries.meaning: Creaky has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I tiptoed down the creaky stairs.
The old door is creakier than ever.
My knees are getting creaky.
The city still runs on a creaky computer system.

senses.head: Making a long, high sound when moved or stepped on
examples: I tiptoed down the creaky stairs.
The old door is creakier than ever.

senses.head: Old and not working well
examples: My knees are getting creaky.
The city still runs on a creaky computer system.

entries.meaning: Pale yellowish-white, the color of cream. ---
examples: She wore a cream-colored sweater.
The walls in the living room are cream-colored.
They chose cream-colored tiles for the bathroom.

entries.meaning: Creamy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The soup is rich and creamy.
This is the creamiest mac and cheese I've ever had.
She has creamy skin and dark hair.
The roses are a creamy white.

senses.head: Thick and smooth, or containing a lot of cream
examples: The soup is rich and creamy.
This is the creamiest mac and cheese I've ever had.

senses.head: Pale yellowish-white and smooth-looking
examples: She has creamy skin and dark hair.
The roses are a creamy white.

entries.meaning: Creative has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She's a very creative cook.
Kids are often more creative than adults.
We need some creative ideas to raise money.
He teaches creative writing at a community college.
She works in the creative department of an ad agency.
The company hid its losses with some creative accounting.
That's a creative way to describe getting fired.

senses.head: Good at thinking of new ideas or making original things
examples: She's a very creative cook.
Kids are often more creative than adults.
We need some creative ideas to raise money.

senses.head: Involving the making of art, writing or music
examples: He teaches creative writing at a community college.
She works in the creative department of an ad agency.

senses.head: Using clever but slightly dishonest ways to change the facts (humorous)
examples: The company hid its losses with some creative accounting.
That's a creative way to describe getting fired.

entries.position: both — senses 2 and 3 only before a noun

entries.meaning: Credible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The witness gave a credible account of the accident.
Her story just isn't credible.
The second report is far more credible than the first.
She's the only credible candidate for the job.
Police said the bomb threat was credible.

senses.head: Able to be believed; convincing
examples: The witness gave a credible account of the accident.
Her story just isn't credible.
The second report is far more credible than the first.

senses.head: Good enough to be taken seriously, as a real competitor or danger
examples: She's the only credible candidate for the job.
Police said the bomb threat was credible.

entries.contrast: The opposite is not incredible, which today usually means amazing. Say not credible or hard to believe. Do not confuse with credulous (too ready to believe).

entries.meaning: Considered safe to lend money to, because likely to pay it back. ---
examples: Banks lend only to creditworthy customers.
A steady job makes you look more creditworthy.
After the losses, the company was no longer creditworthy.

entries.meaning: Too ready to believe what people tell you, and so easily tricked. ---
examples: The scam targeted credulous retirees.
Only the most credulous viewers believed the video was real.
Don't be so credulous; check the facts first.
entries.contrast: Credulous (too ready to believe) is not credible (believable). Incredulous means not able to believe what you see or hear: an incredulous look.

entries.meaning: Creepy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The old house is really creepy at night.
That was the creepiest movie I've ever seen.
Some creepy guy kept staring at her on the train.
It's kind of creepy how much the app knows about me.

senses.head: Strange and frightening, so that you feel nervous
examples: The old house is really creepy at night.
That was the creepiest movie I've ever seen.

senses.head: Unpleasant in a way that makes people uncomfortable, often by showing unwanted interest in them
examples: Some creepy guy kept staring at her on the train.
It's kind of creepy how much the app knows about me.

entries.meaning: Giving you the unpleasant feeling that something is crawling on your skin. ---
examples: The basement has a creepy-crawly feel to it.
Spiders make me all creepy-crawly.
She told the kids a creepy-crawly story around the fire.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for a bug: The kids collect creepy-crawlies in a jar.

entries.meaning: Relating to the Creole people and culture, especially of Louisiana and the Caribbean. ---
examples: The restaurant serves Creole dishes like jambalaya and gumbo.
The French Quarter is full of old Creole townhouses.
His family is Creole, from southern Louisiana.
entries.contrast: A Creole is also a person. A creole, often with a small letter, is a language that grew out of a mix of languages, such as Haitian Creole.

entries.meaning: Sad and disappointed because something has gone wrong. ---
examples: He looked crestfallen when she said no.
The crestfallen players walked slowly off the field.
She seemed even more crestfallen when she saw her grade.

entries.meaning: Criminal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He has no criminal record.
She's a criminal defense lawyer.
Police opened a criminal investigation.
It's criminal that teachers are paid so little.
Throwing away all that good food is criminal.

senses.head: Relating to crime or to the laws about crime
examples: He has no criminal record.
She's a criminal defense lawyer.
Police opened a criminal investigation.

senses.head: Very wrong or shameful; often used to exaggerate (informal)
examples: It's criminal that teachers are paid so little.
Throwing away all that good food is criminal.

entries.position: both — sense 1 only before a noun
entries.contrast: A criminal is also the noun. English uses criminal for both Russian уголовный and криминальный: criminal law, a criminal record, a criminal case.

entries.meaning: Crimson has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She wore a crimson dress to the party.
The maple leaves turn crimson in the fall.
The school colors are crimson and white.
His face went crimson when they laughed.
She turned crimson and looked away.

senses.head: Deep red with a slight purple color
examples: She wore a crimson dress to the party.
The maple leaves turn crimson in the fall.
The school colors are crimson and white.

senses.head: Of a face: red with embarrassment or anger
examples: His face went crimson when they laughed.
She turned crimson and looked away.

entries.meaning: Covered in small folds or lines. ---
examples: She smoothed out the crinkled receipt.
His eyes were crinkled with laughter.
The crinkled old map was hard to read.

entries.meaning: Having many small folds or lines, often making a soft crackling sound. ---
examples: The chips come in a crinkly plastic bag.
Grandpa has a warm, crinkly smile.
The more I folded the map, the crinklier it got.

entries.meaning: Crippled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The storm left the city with a crippled power grid.
Tugboats towed the crippled ship back to port.
The strike hit an already crippled economy.
In old novels, crippled characters are often objects of pity.
We took the crippled bird to a wildlife center.

senses.head: Badly damaged or weakened, so that it cannot work normally
examples: The storm left the city with a crippled power grid.
Tugboats towed the crippled ship back to port.
The strike hit an already crippled economy.

senses.head: Unable to walk or move normally because of injury or illness (now offensive about people)
examples: In old novels, crippled characters are often objects of pity.
We took the crippled bird to a wildlife center.

entries.contrast: Used about people, crippled is now offensive; say disabled or has a disability. About things (a crippled economy, a crippled ship) it is normal.

entries.meaning: So severe that it stops someone or something from working normally. ---
examples: Many graduates face crippling student debt.
She suffers from crippling migraines.
It was the most crippling drought in decades.

entries.meaning: Crisp has 4 distinct senses.
examples: I love a crisp green apple.
Cook the bacon until it's crisp.
It was a crisp fall morning.
The air gets crisper up in the mountains.
He wore a crisp white shirt.
She paid with a crisp twenty-dollar bill.
The new TV has a crisp picture.
Her answers were short and crisp.

senses.head: Firm and dry, so it breaks with a pleasant sound when you bite it
examples: I love a crisp green apple.
Cook the bacon until it's crisp.

senses.head: Of weather or air: cold, dry and fresh
examples: It was a crisp fall morning.
The air gets crisper up in the mountains.

senses.head: Of paper or cloth: fresh, clean and smooth
examples: He wore a crisp white shirt.
She paid with a crisp twenty-dollar bill.

senses.head: Clear, sharp and quick, with nothing extra
examples: The new TV has a crisp picture.
Her answers were short and crisp.

entries.contrast: A crisp is British for a potato chip; Americans say chip. Crisp and crispy overlap for food, but for weather, clothes, money and pictures use only crisp.

entries.meaning: Pleasantly hard and crunchy, especially of fried or baked food. ---
examples: I like my fries extra crispy.
The chicken has a crispy golden crust.
Pizza comes out crispier in the oven than in the microwave.
entries.contrast: Use crispy for cooked food. Fresh fruit and vegetables are usually crisp, and so are weather, clothes and bills.

entries.meaning: Critical has 5 distinct senses.
examples: Her boss is very critical of her work.
He made some critical comments about the plan.
The newspapers were even more critical the next day.
The next few days are critical.
Clean water is critical to good health.
Timing is the most critical part of the plan.
The driver is in critical condition at the hospital.
The shortage of nurses has reached a critical point.
The course teaches critical thinking.
Read the article with a critical eye.
The movie was a critical success but lost money.
Her first novel won critical acclaim.

senses.head: Saying that someone or something is bad or wrong
examples: Her boss is very critical of her work.
He made some critical comments about the plan.
The newspapers were even more critical the next day.

senses.head: Extremely important, because a lot depends on it
examples: The next few days are critical.
Clean water is critical to good health.
Timing is the most critical part of the plan.

senses.head: Very serious or dangerous, especially of an illness or situation
examples: The driver is in critical condition at the hospital.
The shortage of nurses has reached a critical point.

senses.head: Judging something carefully to see what is good or bad about it
examples: The course teaches critical thinking.
Read the article with a critical eye.

senses.head: Relating to the opinions of critics about books, movies or art
examples: The movie was a critical success but lost money.
Her first novel won critical acclaim.

entries.position: both — senses 4 and 5 only before a noun
entries.takes: of + noun (sense 1); to or for + noun (sense 2)
entries.contrast: Not every critical is negative: a critical role and critical information mean very important. In American news, in critical condition means in danger of dying.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Croatia, its people or its language. ---
examples: We spent a week on the Croatian coast.
My wife is Croatian.
He learned a few Croatian songs from his grandmother.
entries.contrast: A Croatian is also a person, also called a Croat. Croatian is also the name of the language.

entries.meaning: Crooked has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Your tie is crooked.
He gave me a crooked smile.
The picture looks more crooked than before.
A crooked cop was taking money from drug dealers.
The whole deal seemed crooked to me.

senses.head: Not straight; bent or twisted
examples: Your tie is crooked.
He gave me a crooked smile.
The picture looks more crooked than before.

senses.head: Dishonest, especially involved in crime (informal)
examples: A crooked cop was taking money from drug dealers.
The whole deal seemed crooked to me.

entries.contrast: The adjective is always two syllables, KRUUK-id, like naked and wicked. The past tense of the verb (she crooked her finger) is one syllable: krukt.

entries.meaning: Cropped has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He has closely cropped gray hair.
Her cropped hair made her look younger.
She wore a cropped jacket over her dress.
Cropped pants are popular this summer.
He posted a cropped photo that left out his ex.
The cropped image looks better on the website.

senses.head: Of hair or grass: cut very short
examples: He has closely cropped gray hair.
Her cropped hair made her look younger.

senses.head: Of clothes: shorter than usual, ending above the waist or the ankle
examples: She wore a cropped jacket over her dress.
Cropped pants are popular this summer.

senses.head: Of a picture: with the edges cut off
examples: He posted a cropped photo that left out his ex.
The cropped image looks better on the website.

entries.meaning: Annoyed or a little angry. ---
examples: Are you cross with me?
She was cross about the mess in the kitchen.
The longer we waited, the crosser he got.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: she was cross
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — crosser, crossest; more cross
entries.contrast: More common in British English. Americans understand it and meet it in books, but usually say mad, annoyed or upset. Cross is also a noun and a verb.

entries.meaning: Involving or comparing two or more different cultures. ---
examples: The company offers cross-cultural training for staff moving abroad.
She studies cross-cultural communication.
Cross-cultural marriages are more common than they used to be.

entries.meaning: Having eyes that turn in toward the nose. ---
examples: The cross-eyed cat became famous online.
She went cross-eyed trying to see the tip of her nose.
Reading all that fine print made me cross-eyed.

entries.meaning: Cross-sectional has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The researchers did a cross-sectional study of 5,000 adults.
Cross-sectional data cannot show cause and effect.
The pipe has a cross-sectional area of two square inches.
The textbook shows a cross-sectional view of the heart.

senses.head: Of research: studying a group of people at one point in time
examples: The researchers did a cross-sectional study of 5,000 adults.
Cross-sectional data cannot show cause and effect.

senses.head: Relating to a cross section, the flat surface you see when you cut straight through something
examples: The pipe has a cross-sectional area of two square inches.
The textbook shows a cross-sectional view of the heart.

entries.meaning: Going from one side of a city to the other. ---
examples: Take the cross-town bus to the East Side.
Traffic made my cross-town commute an hour long.
The two high schools are cross-town rivals.
entries.contrast: Americans usually write it as one word, crosstown. It is also an adverb: we drove crosstown.

entries.meaning: Easily annoyed and always complaining, especially of an old person. ---
examples: A crotchety old man lives next door.
Grandpa gets crotchety when his back hurts.
He grew more crotchety with every passing year.

entries.meaning: Crowded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The subway is always crowded at rush hour.

Downtown is more crowded on weekends.
I have a very crowded schedule this week.
The market for electric cars is getting crowded.

senses.head: Full of people, with little room to move
examples: The subway is always crowded at rush hour.

Downtown is more crowded on weekends.

senses.head: Having too many things or events in a small space or time
examples: I have a very crowded schedule this week.
The market for electric cars is getting crowded.

entries.meaning: Being the best or most important part of something. ---
examples: The bridge was the engineer's crowning achievement.
Winning the title was the crowning moment of his career.
The crowning touch was a single cherry on top.

entries.meaning: Dirty, unpleasant or of poor quality (informal, milder than crappy). ---
examples: I'm stuck with a cruddy old laptop.

It was the cruddiest motel on the highway.

senses.head: Of oil and other materials: in a natural state, before being processed

entries.meaning: Easily breaking into small pieces. ---

entries.meaning: Bad, cheap or of poor quality (informal). ---

senses.head: Pressed or broken into very small pieces
examples: I'd like a soda with crushed ice.
Add two cloves of crushed garlic.
The path is covered with crushed stone.

senses.head: Extremely sad and disappointed
examples: She was crushed when she didn't get the part.
He looked crushed after the loss.

entries.position: both — sense 2 mostly after a verb
entries.contrast: Have a crush on someone (be attracted to them) uses the noun crush, not this adjective.

entries.meaning: Very severe; causing great damage, defeat or disappointment. ---
examples: The team suffered a crushing defeat.
Losing her job was a crushing blow.
It was the most crushing loss in the team's history.

entries.meaning: Having a hidden or unclear meaning; hard to understand. ---
examples: He left a cryptic note on the fridge.
Her answer was short and cryptic.
His texts are getting more cryptic every day.

entries.meaning: Relating to writing or breaking secret codes, especially to protect computer data. ---
examples: Every message is protected with a cryptographic key.
The bank updated its cryptographic software.
Researchers found a flaw in the cryptographic protocol.

entries.meaning: Crystal clear has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We swam in crystal-clear water.
The lake is crystal clear in the morning.
The new speakers give crystal-clear sound.
Let me make this crystal clear: no phones in class.
The message from voters was crystal clear.

senses.head: Of water, air, glass or sound: completely clear
examples: We swam in crystal-clear water.
The lake is crystal clear in the morning.
The new speakers give crystal-clear sound.

senses.head: Very easy to understand; completely obvious
examples: Let me make this crystal clear: no phones in class.
The message from voters was crystal clear.

entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun: crystal-clear water

entries.meaning: Crystallized has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Warm the jar to soften crystallized honey.
Crystallized salt covered the rocks by the shore.
The cake was topped with crystallized ginger.
She makes crystallized orange peel every December.

senses.head: Turned into crystals
examples: Warm the jar to soften crystallized honey.
Crystallized salt covered the rocks by the shore.

senses.head: Of fruit: cooked in sugar and covered with sugar crystals
examples: The cake was topped with crystallized ginger.
She makes crystallized orange peel every December.

entries.contrast: British spelling is crystallised. For fruit Americans more often say candied: candied ginger.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Cuba. ---
examples: We ate Cuban sandwiches in Miami.
His parents are Cuban.
She loves old Cuban music.
entries.contrast: A Cuban is also a person from Cuba, and in Florida it can mean a pressed ham-and-pork sandwich.

entries.meaning: Cubic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The fridge has 20 cubic feet of space.
We ordered ten cubic yards of mulch.
The engine is 1,500 cubic centimeters.
The museum is a large cubic building of glass.
Salt forms tiny cubic crystals.

senses.head: Used in measuring volume: equal to a cube whose sides are the given length
examples: The fridge has 20 cubic feet of space.
We ordered ten cubic yards of mulch.
The engine is 1,500 cubic centimeters.

senses.head: Shaped like a cube
examples: The museum is a large cubic building of glass.
Salt forms tiny cubic crystals.

entries.meaning: Soft, warm and pleasant to hug. ---
examples: The baby hugged her cuddly teddy bear.
Puppies are so cuddly.
Our new cat is much cuddlier than the old one.

entries.meaning: Relating to cooking. ---
examples: She went to culinary school in New York.
He's proud of his culinary skills.
New Orleans is famous for its culinary traditions.

entries.meaning: Deserving blame for something wrong (formal). ---
examples: Both drivers were partly culpable for the accident.
The report found the company culpable for the spill.
In my view, the managers were more culpable than the workers.

entries.meaning: Cultivated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Only a small part of the valley is cultivated land.
Cultivated mushrooms are cheaper than wild ones.
She's a cultivated woman who loves opera.
His voice sounded more cultivated than his clothes suggested.

senses.head: Of land or plants: used for growing crops, or grown by farmers rather than wild
examples: Only a small part of the valley is cultivated land.
Cultivated mushrooms are cheaper than wild ones.

senses.head: Well educated, with good taste and manners
examples: She's a cultivated woman who loves opera.
His voice sounded more cultivated than his clothes suggested.

entries.comparison: more/most — sense 2: more cultivated, most cultivated
entries.contrast: For an educated, well-mannered person, Russian культурный is cultured or cultivated, never cultural.

entries.meaning: Cultural has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Moving abroad meant getting used to cultural differences.
The festival celebrates the city's cultural diversity.
Some of the problems are cultural, not economic.
Chicago has a rich cultural life.
The new cultural center has a theater and a gallery.

senses.head: Relating to the customs, beliefs and way of life of a group of people
examples: Moving abroad meant getting used to cultural differences.
The festival celebrates the city's cultural diversity.
Some of the problems are cultural, not economic.

senses.head: Relating to art, music, literature and theater
examples: Chicago has a rich cultural life.
The new cultural center has a theater and a gallery.

entries.contrast: Cultural never describes a person's manners. Культурный человек is a cultured person or a well-mannered person; a cultural person is wrong.

entries.meaning: Cultured has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's a cultured man who reads in three languages.
A year in Paris made her feel more cultured.
She wore a string of cultured pearls.
The recipe calls for cultured buttermilk.

senses.head: Well educated and interested in art, music and literature
examples: He's a cultured man who reads in three languages.
A year in Paris made her feel more cultured.

senses.head: Grown or made using living cells or bacteria under controlled conditions
examples: She wore a string of cultured pearls.
The recipe calls for cultured buttermilk.

entries.position: both — sense 2 only before a noun
entries.comparison: more/most — sense 1: more cultured, most cultured
entries.contrast: Not cultural: a cultured person, but cultural events.

entries.meaning: Of a degree or a graduate: awarded with honors. ---
examples: He's a cum laude graduate of Ohio State.
Cum laude honors take a 3.5 average here.
She hung her cum laude diploma over the desk.
entries.position: attributive only — a cum laude graduate; after a verb it is an adverb: she graduated cum laude
entries.form: Latin — 'with praise'; stronger: magna cum laude, summa cum laude
entries.contrast: Keep the Latin phrase in two words and never add -er or very. The higher honors are magna cum laude and summa cum laude.

entries.meaning: Cumbersome has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The old cameras were cumbersome to carry.
We finally got rid of that cumbersome sofa.
The application process is cumbersome.
The new rules are even more cumbersome than the old ones.

senses.head: Large and heavy, and so hard to carry or use
examples: The old cameras were cumbersome to carry.
We finally got rid of that cumbersome sofa.

senses.head: Slow and complicated
examples: The application process is cumbersome.
The new rules are even more cumbersome than the old ones.

entries.meaning: Increasing over time as each new amount is added. ---
examples: The cumulative effect of small changes can be huge.
Her cumulative GPA is 3.8.
The damage to his hearing was cumulative.

entries.meaning: Clever at getting what you want, especially by tricking people. ---
examples: The villain in the movie is cunning and cruel.
They came up with a cunning plan to avoid paying taxes.
The fox is supposed to be the most cunning animal in the forest.
entries.contrast: Cunning is not simple praise: it means clever in a sly, often dishonest way. For clever in a good sense say smart or clever. In older American books cunning can also mean cute (a cunning little hat).

entries.meaning: Able to be cured. ---
examples: The disease is curable if it's caught early.
Doctors now treat it as a curable condition.
Skin cancer is more curable than many other cancers.

entries.meaning: Able to cure an illness, or meant to. ---
examples: Some people believe in the curative powers of honey.
The town was famous for its curative hot springs.
The treatment is not curative, but it eases the pain.

entries.meaning: Of milk or a sauce, separated into lumps, usually because it has gone sour or been overheated. ---
examples: The milk in the fridge was curdled.
Don't boil the sauce or you'll end up with a curdled mess.
The creamer came out curdled, so I threw it away.

entries.meaning: Cured has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The deli sells Italian cured meats.
She served cured salmon on rye bread.
Bacon is cured pork belly.
After six months of treatment, she was completely cured.
I thought I was cured of my fear of flying, but I wasn't.

senses.head: Of meat or fish, preserved by salting, smoking or drying
examples: The deli sells Italian cured meats.
She served cured salmon on rye bread.
Bacon is cured pork belly.

senses.head: Healed of an illness, or free of a problem
examples: After six months of treatment, she was completely cured.
I thought I was cured of my fear of flying, but I wasn't.

entries.takes: of + noun (sense 2: cured of his fear)

entries.meaning: Twisted into rings or curves, or bent into a round shape. ---
examples: She had long, curled hair for the wedding.
The cat lay curled up by the fire.
The old photo had curled edges.
entries.contrast: Curly hair grows that way; curled hair has been styled with an iron or rollers.

entries.meaning: Bad-tempered and easily annoyed, especially in an old person. ---
examples: Our curmudgeonly neighbor yells at kids who step on his lawn.
He's curmudgeonly, but he has a good heart.
My grandpa got more curmudgeonly every year.
entries.contrast: It ends in -ly but is an adjective, not an adverb.

entries.meaning: Current has 2 distinct senses.
examples: What's your current address?
The current mayor took office in January.
Prices are high in the current economy.
You need a current passport to fly.
Are you current on your rent?
This map is the most current one we have.

senses.head: Happening or existing now
examples: What's your current address?
The current mayor took office in January.
Prices are high in the current economy.

senses.head: Up to date, or still valid
examples: You need a current passport to fly.
Are you current on your rent?
This map is the most current one we have.

entries.comparison: not gradable — except sense 2: more current, most current
entries.takes: on or with + noun (sense 2: current on your payments)
entries.contrast: Currently is the adverb (She currently lives in Denver). Current is also a noun: an electric current, an ocean current. Russian актуальный is often relevant or topical, not current.

entries.meaning: Cursed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The locals say the old house is cursed.
Some fans believe the team is cursed.
Nobody wanted to buy the cursed ring.
She was cursed with terrible luck.
He's cursed with a bad back.

senses.head: Under a curse, so that bad things keep happening
examples: The locals say the old house is cursed.
Some fans believe the team is cursed.
Nobody wanted to buy the cursed ring.

senses.head: Suffering from something bad that you cannot get rid of
examples: She was cursed with terrible luck.
He's cursed with a bad back.

entries.contrast: Before a noun it is often KUR-sid (a cursed house); in cursed with it is KURST. Cursed is also the past of the verb curse (He cursed loudly).

entries.meaning: Of handwriting, with the letters joined together. ---
examples: Grandma's letters were written in beautiful cursive script.
She signed her name in cursive letters.
Many schools stopped teaching cursive handwriting.
entries.contrast: A false friend: cursive is joined-up handwriting, not курсив. Slanted print is italics. Cursive is also a noun: Kids don't learn cursive anymore.

entries.meaning: Done quickly, without much attention to detail. ---
examples: He gave the report only a cursory glance.
After a cursory search, the police left.
The inspection was cursory at best.

entries.meaning: Rudely short in speech or manner. ---
examples: She gave a curt reply and hung up.
He was curt with the waiter.
His emails got more curt as the deadline approached.

entries.meaning: Having attractive curves, usually said of a woman's body, sometimes of a car or other object. ---
examples: The actress was known for her curvaceous figure.
The car's curvaceous body turned heads.
The new model is more curvaceous than the old boxy one.

entries.meaning: Curvy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We drove along a curvy mountain road.
The chair has a curvy back.
This is the curviest stretch of the highway.
The store sells jeans for curvy women.
She's curvier than her sister.

senses.head: Having many curves or bends
examples: We drove along a curvy mountain road.
The chair has a curvy back.
This is the curviest stretch of the highway.

senses.head: Of a woman, having a full figure with noticeable hips and breasts
examples: The store sells jeans for curvy women.
She's curvier than her sister.

entries.meaning: Soft and padded, so it protects you from hard contact. ---
examples: The chairs have cushioned seats.
We sat on a cushioned bench by the window.
These running shoes are more cushioned than my old ones.

entries.meaning: Easy and comfortable, needing little effort; informal. ---
examples: He has a cushy job at his uncle's firm.
Life in the suburbs was pretty cushy.
She landed the cushiest assignment in the office.

entries.meaning: Custodial has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The custodial parent decides where the child goes to school.
She was granted custodial rights after the divorce.
The confession came during a custodial interrogation.
Several deaths in custodial settings are under investigation.
The school hired more custodial staff.
Custodial services are included in the rent.

senses.head: Having legal custody of a child
examples: The custodial parent decides where the child goes to school.
She was granted custodial rights after the divorce.

senses.head: Involving being held in prison or by the police
examples: The confession came during a custodial interrogation.
Several deaths in custodial settings are under investigation.

senses.head: Relating to cleaning and taking care of a building
examples: The school hired more custodial staff.
Custodial services are included in the rent.

entries.русский: опекунский; связанный с содержанием под стражей; хозяйственный
entries.contrast: In American English custodian is also the polite word for a janitor, so custodial staff are the people who clean a school or office.

entries.meaning: Made or done to a particular customer's order. ---
examples: They have a custom kitchen with walnut cabinets.
The shop does custom paint jobs.
You can order custom T-shirts with your team's logo.
entries.contrast: The noun custom means a tradition (обычай), and customs is the check at the border (таможня). The adjective custom is American; British English prefers bespoke or made-to-measure.

entries.meaning: Built to a particular customer's order. ---
examples: They live in a custom-built house by the lake.
His guitar was custom-built in Nashville.
The company makes custom-built computers for gamers.

entries.meaning: Made to a particular customer's order or measurements. ---
examples: He wore a custom-made suit to the wedding.
The boots were custom-made for her.
We ordered custom-made curtains for the big windows.

entries.meaning: Usual, according to custom or habit. ---
examples: It is customary to tip 15 to 20 percent in restaurants.
He took his customary seat at the end of the table.
In some cultures, it's more customary to bow than to shake hands.
entries.takes: it is customary to + infinitive; for someone to do

entries.meaning: Cut has 3 distinct senses.
examples: A vase of fresh cut flowers stood on the table.
The yard smelled of freshly cut grass.
The chandelier was made of cut crystal.
He wore a well-cut gray suit.
She wore a beautifully cut diamond.
He's been lifting weights, and he's really cut.
She got even more cut before the competition.

senses.head: Removed from the plant by cutting
examples: A vase of fresh cut flowers stood on the table.
The yard smelled of freshly cut grass.

senses.head: Shaped by cutting, like glass, a gem or a piece of clothing
examples: The chandelier was made of cut crystal.
He wore a well-cut gray suit.
She wore a beautifully cut diamond.

senses.head: Having muscles that show clearly, with very little fat
examples: He's been lifting weights, and he's really cut.
She got even more cut before the competition.

entries.comparison: not gradable — except sense 3, informally more cut
entries.contrast: He cut his hand is the verb. In the muscle sense cut is informal American slang, like ripped.

entries.meaning: Simple and clear, with no room for doubt or argument. ---
examples: The case isn't as cut-and-dried as it looks.
There's no cut-and-dried answer to that question.
For the judge, it was all pretty cut-and-dried.
entries.contrast: Mostly used with a negative: It's not that cut-and-dried. After a verb it is often written without hyphens: The case is cut and dried.

entries.meaning: Sold at a reduced price, and often of low quality. ---
examples: They sell cut-rate airline tickets online.
He bought a cut-rate phone that broke in a week.
Don't trust a cut-rate contractor with your roof.

entries.meaning: Cute has 3 distinct senses.
examples: What a cute puppy!
That's the cutest baby I've ever seen.
Your little house is so cute.
There's a cute guy in my chemistry class.
Do you think he's cuter than his brother?
Don't get cute with me — just answer the question.
That was a cute trick, but it won't work twice.

senses.head: Pretty and charming, especially a baby, a small animal or a small thing
examples: What a cute puppy!
That's the cutest baby I've ever seen.
Your little house is so cute.

senses.head: Sexually attractive
examples: There's a cute guy in my chemistry class.
Do you think he's cuter than his brother?

senses.head: Clever in a way that is annoying or not quite honest
examples: Don't get cute with me — just answer the question.
That was a cute trick, but it won't work twice.

entries.contrast: Said of an adult in American English, cute usually means attractive (a cute guy), not only sweet like a baby. Said with an edge (Don't get cute with me), it means too clever or cheeky.

entries.meaning: Ready to do anything to win, with no concern for others. ---
examples: They faced cutthroat competition from the big chains.
The restaurant business is cutthroat.
Wall Street was the most cutthroat place I've ever worked.

entries.meaning: Cutting has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She made a cutting remark about his weight.
His review of the film was cutting.
It was the most cutting thing anyone had ever said to her.
A cutting wind blew off the lake.
The cold was cutting that morning.

senses.head: Unkind and meant to hurt someone's feelings
examples: She made a cutting remark about his weight.
His review of the film was cutting.
It was the most cutting thing anyone had ever said to her.

senses.head: Of wind or cold, sharp and unpleasant
examples: A cutting wind blew off the lake.
The cold was cutting that morning.

entries.contrast: A cutting is also a noun: a piece cut from a plant to grow a new one. Don't confuse it with cutting-edge.

entries.meaning: The newest and most advanced. ---
examples: The lab uses cutting-edge technology.
Their design is really cutting-edge.
It's the most cutting-edge phone on the market.
entries.contrast: Hyphenated as an adjective (cutting-edge research). At the cutting edge of is the noun phrase, with no hyphen.

entries.meaning: Happening in cycles, repeating the same pattern again and again. ---
examples: The housing market is cyclical.
Some historians see a cyclical pattern in history.
Some industries are more cyclical than others.

entries.meaning: Shaped like a cylinder, long and round. ---
examples: The oil is stored in cylindrical tanks.
A soda can has a cylindrical shape.
The old water tower is cylindrical.

entries.meaning: Cynical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Many voters are cynical about politicians.
After years in the news business, he became more cynical.
Don't be so cynical — some people really do want to help.
It was a cynical attempt to win votes.
The company made a cynical decision to hide the risks.

senses.head: Believing that people act only out of selfishness, and distrusting their motives
examples: Many voters are cynical about politicians.
After years in the news business, he became more cynical.
Don't be so cynical — some people really do want to help.

senses.head: Done for selfish reasons, with no concern for what is right
examples: It was a cynical attempt to win votes.
The company made a cynical decision to hide the risks.

entries.contrast: Partly a false friend. English cynical mostly means distrustful, expecting the worst of people. Russian циничный often suggests shameless or crude; for that, say crude or shameless.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Cyprus. ---
examples: Halloumi is a traditional Cypriot cheese.
Her mother is Cypriot.
The Cypriot government announced new rules for tourists.
entries.contrast: A Cypriot is also a person from Cyprus. The country is Cyprus.

entries.meaning: Relating to the alphabet used for Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian and other languages. ---
examples: Russian is written in the Cyrillic alphabet.
The sign was in Cyrillic letters, so I couldn't read it.
My keyboard has both Latin and Cyrillic characters.
entries.contrast: Always with a capital C. It is also a noun: Can you read Cyrillic?

entries.meaning: Relating to the czars or their government in Russia before 1917. ---
examples: The family fled czarist Russia in 1905.
Under czarist rule, most peasants could not read.
The museum has a collection of czarist coins.
entries.contrast: Also spelled tsarist. It means of the czars, not magnificent: for царский прием say a lavish welcome.

entries.meaning: From or relating to the Czech Republic, its people or its language. ---
examples: Prague is famous for Czech beer.
My grandparents were Czech.
She's taking a Czech class at the community college.
entries.contrast: Pronounced like check. The language is Czech, the people are Czechs, and the country is the Czech Republic or Czechia.

entries.meaning: From or relating to the former country of Czechoslovakia.
examples: He played on the Czechoslovakian national hockey team in the 1980s.
The film is a Czechoslovakian classic from the 1960s.
Her passport was still Czechoslovakian when she came to the U.S.
entries.contrast: Historical: Czechoslovakia split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993. Czechoslovak means the same.
